# In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. May God bless our master and leader Muhammad.

## The Letter Ha (ح)

**Thyme** <note>original: *Hasha* (حاشا); likely *Thymus capitatus* or a related species</note> ∴ The herbalists of Andalusia and the common folk know it as "Donkey’s Thyme." It is abundant in the land of Jerusalem and its surrounding areas. Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> states in the third book: *Thymos* <note>original Greek: *thumos*</note> is the *Hasha* known to all people. It is a small shrub, the branches of which are of a size suitable for twisting into lamp wicks. It has many small, slender leaves, and at its tips are small heads of purple flowers. It grows mostly in rocky places and thin soil. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> states in the sixth book: Thyme cuts through <note>meaning it thins thick humors</note> and warms with a distinct heat. For this reason, it promotes menstruation and urine, expels fetuses, opens obstructions of the internal organs, and is beneficial for coughing up matter from the chest and lungs. Because of this, it should be classified in the third degree of drying and heating. Dioscorides says: If drunk with salt and vinegar, it purges phlegmatic chyme <note>term: *chyme* (the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food)</note>. When its decoction is used with honey, it benefits orthopnea <note>difficulty breathing unless standing or sitting upright</note>, asthma, and the expulsion of long worms. It promotes menstruation and the expulsion of the fetus and the afterbirth. It is a diuretic. If kneaded with honey and licked <note>as an electuary</note>, it eases some of the waste fluids in the chest. If applied as a poultice with vinegar, it dissolves recent phlegmatic swellings. It dissolves clotted blood and removes pustules and the warts known as *Aprochordon* <note>original: *afrokhurdun*, from the Greek *achrochordon*</note>. If mixed with parched barley flour, kneaded with wine, and placed on the sciatic nerve, it is beneficial. If added to food and eaten, it benefits weakness of sight. It is suitable for use during times of health. Masarjawaih <note>A 7th-century Persian Jewish physician</note> says: It cleanses the liver and the stomach. If crushed and kneaded with water and honey, and two *mithqals* <note>term: *mithqal* (a unit of weight, approx. 4.25 grams)</note> are drunk, it benefits colic, dissolves waste fluids, strengthens the kidneys, and stimulates sexual intercourse. Al-Dimashqi says: It benefits pain of the mouth and throat and everything that Epithyme <note>original: *athymaun*</note> benefits, though it is lesser than Epithyme. Ibn Sarabiun <note>Serapion the Elder, a 9th-century Syrian physician</note> says: The flower of Thyme purges black bile, but it is weak; therefore, it should be mixed with salt. Some people give it with vinegar to increase its thinning effect. The dose of its flower is two *mithqals* with vinegar and water. The heads of Thyme and Savory <note>original: *sa'tar*</note> remove darkness from the vision and thin the phlegm; Thyme is stronger than Savory in that regard. Dioscorides says in the fifth book: The description of the wine made with Thyme—the method of its preparation is to crush the medicine, sift it, take one hundred *mithqals* of it, place it in a cloth, and cast it into a jar of grape juice. This wine benefits...

# Morning Glory Seed
<note>original: "Hubb al-Nil" (Ipomoea nil). Historically used as a potent purgative.</note>

...due to what it generates of winds and bloating, it is hot and dry. In its seed is the power of the **Morning Glory Seed**, the purgative. The essence of the purgative dose is three *dirhams* and thirteen *kirats* <note>approx. 12 grams</note>. Its maximum limit is five *dirhams*. It is said its essence is hot and dry in the second degree. In the eighth <unclear>degree</unclear>, a single seed is hot and dry. It thickens the fetus <unclear>preventing</unclear> fainting. Taken in its response is the evacuation of phlegm and black bile, specifically through light and gentle preparation. It stops watery catarrh and hernia. Among them, that which was fresh and dry <insert>is best</insert>, and perhaps it does not cause fainting. What was spread of it or forgotten becomes a thin sediment. Up to the second <unclear>degree</unclear>, the seed is a purgative for yellow bile. For children, taking its vinegar in the amount of four *dirhams* is sufficient. It is tested in it to use a paste thickened with lettuce water as a dyed stuffing. In the braying <note>sound of the gut</note> which it eases, it is mastered by the power of a sedative. It overcomes the heat of its safety and strips <unclear>the lining</unclear>, killing by its specific property within twenty-four hours. It is hot, dry, and sharp in application. Its purgative power is aided by the end, and in it, it extracts phlegm and twice extracts yellow bile. Perhaps a stickiness from lethargy afflicts him. Its end is suppression, and it lowers the phlegm of the stomach and colic; it is a diuretic. If one eats of its seeds, it causes vomiting. It may cause lacerations in the stomach. The amount of a drink of it with others is one hundred and twenty seeds, and perhaps it reaches fifty. You lighten it with honey-water and a drop of it as needed. As for what benefits us in it, even the transition of a dog from its evil <note>possibly referring to rabies or canine aggression</note>, its actions and branches on the hand are clarified. It was said it dries <margin>Potash Seed</margin> hemorrhoids and the vulva. If the stone is <unclear>leached</unclear>, it is stronger than the second degree. In its benefit, its weight is half an ointment, and the hope of its drying with water is more effective for the hemorrhoid.

### Kidney Seed
<note>original: "Hubb al-Kula". Likely refers to Anagyris foetida or a similar bean-shaped seed.</note>
The purgative in it is the essence of the kidneys. It has a pleasant scent and green spring flowers. The "Star of the Kidneys" is its most wonderful form. It is called in Greek *Anagyris*. Moving it brings out the seed for the kidneys. Among the physicians of the "corruptor" <note>referring to a specific medical school or text</note>, it is called in Greek *Anagyris*. From its blessing, the seed emerges. It is not the "treacherous seed" mentioned by Ibn Ridwan <note>Egyptian physician, d. 1061 AD</note> which he says takes to the air except by a single gulp. Distinguish the "Chosen Seed of Zalm" <note>Cyperus esculentus</note> as it requires the seed to emerge from the flesh slightly. In the months of the word, the "White of Wealth" is **Cress Seed** <note>Hubb al-Rashad</note>, because its nature is to destroy leprosy from the water. Even in the mirror, it preserves it, and its black nature in the eyes of cattle which dries the wound significantly.

### Mastic Seed
<note>original: "Hubb al-Masm". Likely refers to the berries of the Mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus) or a similar aromatic seed.</note>
The *Masm* is a name for a seed found abundantly in Yemen; it necessitates the removal of grief through its heat and fineness. It is finer than cinnamon and myrrh, and it is the most cunning of foods. Mentioned in its four <unclear>sides</unclear>, the growth from it is highly aromatic. Its power in the temperament is in its remainder, and benefit occurred from it for the "Indian Praises." It enters into the thicket of those who love women. As for its mixing, the most who use it are the refined people of Yemen and the people of the Hijaz, and it is softer among the people of Iraq, and less so in Egypt and the Levant. It is, according to the people of India and the <unclear>Gezira</unclear>, praised and found in the interior of the Levant, beneficial for the cold stomach filled with defects. A weight of one *jund* <note>a small weight measure</note> is used in the bath, or upon leaving it; it is milked and then its trace is stuffed to heal the owner. 

**The Mother of Hani Stone** <note>original: "حجر أم الهني" – likely a type of Bezoar</note> is a proven remedy. It forms in the gallbladder of a cow as a soft, beautiful image. It comes out of the gallbladder while it is moist, soft, and smooth. Its color is like a cooked egg, then it solidifies and thickens until it reaches the consistency of a royal crust.

# Treatments from the Earth and the Field

The wild [variety] should be consumed with Magnesia stone <gloss>Magnesia</gloss> <note>original: "مغنيسيا" - likely magnesium carbonate or a similar mineral used as a laxative</note> in honey-water, for it purifies the body of foul humors and wind in the stomach. **Arugula** <note>original: "الجرجير" (Eruca sativa)</note> is beneficial for stimulating the libido, increases the semen, and causes a sensation of fullness in the mouth and stomach. At the onset of a wound, [a poultice] should be applied. For the eye, milk should be used alongside potent virtues. Then, the lime used for cauterization should be bound with water <gloss>its kunyah <note>a descriptive name</note> is "Khuramah" from Agrimony</gloss>.

As for Arugula, it is hot and dry in the second degree; it generates headaches in the head, yet its seeds provide relief from dysentery <note>original: "زحير" - tenesmus or painful straining</note> and act as an astringent. 

As for **Germander** <note>original: "الجعدة" - plants of the Teucrium genus</note>, it has a bitter, sharp taste. It is beneficial against [intestinal] worms when mixed with vinegar. It relieves a bloated stomach and heals tumors quickly. It promotes urination and menstruation, and provides strength. It is used for sores forming in the mouth and for hemorrhoids growing in the anus—by the power of God Almighty. When cooked and applied to a swelling, it is beneficial. It also heals severe "sheep-scab" <note>likely a skin condition like psoriasis or eczema</note> and the inflammation of "the Redness" <note>original: "الحمرة" - Erysipelas, a bacterial skin infection</note>. In Greek, it is called *Androsaces* <margin>Androsaces</margin> <note>original: "اند برياكس" - a transliteration of the Greek 'androsakes'</note>. Its stem is like a burnt stalk without leaves <gloss>Androsaces</gloss>. This species is bare and fiery in nature, acting upon the stomach. Its heat draws the blood and renews the "winds" <note>internal gases or spirits</note> that oppose the nerves. If its sharpness is tempered with a little oil, it treats headaches and migraines.

<margin>The Wild Rue</margin>
From the seeds of the *Nadr* and the heat of the [plant], if mixed with leeks and honey and drunk by one suffering from dysentery or hemorrhoids, it is beneficial. If the head of the plant is burnt and mixed with water during the [rainy] period, it helps those with labored breathing. Three fingers' width [of the medicine] should be applied over the head. The bitterness of the plant, if kneaded with raw oil or mixed with water, peels away the scales of leprosy and heals spots. It is effective for stings in the Levant <note>Greater Syria</note>. It is also used as a wash for the eyes to treat epilepsy. In three days, it heals every hundred [afflictions], God Almighty willing. If placed in a vessel, it is better; it treats the "Yellow Wind" <margin>Yellow Bile</margin> <note>original: "الريح الصفراء" - often referring to jaundice or bilious disorders</note>.

**Hobakj** of the mountain: when its leaves are burnt, it treats tumors. In the *Book of Plants* by Abu al-Abbas al-Nabati <note>A famous 13th-century Andalusian botanist and teacher of Ibn al-Baitar</note>, it is recorded in Arabic as *Dafhar*. This is a name for a type of Hijazi plant that twines around palm trees. Its clusters are not large, and its liquid is pressed until it becomes [thick]. Its fruit is first green, then ripens and turns the size and shape of a walnut. The plant has black fruit, branches, and leaves. Some varieties grow in Yemen and are known as *al-Murrah* and *Bariq*.

<column-break/>

<margin>Epilepsy</margin>
**Epilepsy**: This [remedy] is hot in the second degree and is beneficial for epilepsy. Bee bile <note>gall</note> is useful for the film and darkness that occurs in the eye, especially if mixed with honey and dropped into the eye. It is hot and dry in the twentieth degree <note>this likely refers to a specific grading scale in medieval pharmacy</note> from the start of the medicine suitable for this eye. If the heat of the skin intensifies each month, [it must be treated].

<margin>Scrofula is sharp and good for its purpose</margin>
Among the beneficial things for ulcers and sores is its topical application. As for mixing the heat of cupping for [the joints], it benefits the joints, headaches, and "white spots" in the eye and nose, and nausea <margin>Sciatica</margin> <note>original: "عرق النساء" - literally 'vein of the women,' the historical term for sciatica</note>. It treats the "clothing of the eye" <note>perhaps a cataract or pannus</note>, night blindness, and scabies. It is beneficial for chest pain and is bound upon large wounds <margin>For Hemorrhoids</margin>. 

For scrofula <note>original: "خنازير" - literally 'pigs,' the common term for tubercular swelling of the lymph nodes</note>, apply it mixed with seeds. The "strips of the palm" are useful for wounds—as proven by experience and [divine] power—especially for wounds at the back of the neck that burn in the lymph nodes. The bile and the [substance] become firm in the "stroke of the viscous" <note>unclear medical term, possibly referring to a type of paralysis or thick humor</note>. 

Dioscorides said regarding the "Locust-plant": "It has many substances and its types vary. Some are soft, some hold water, and some are firm in strength." Some grow at the base of mountains. People use it as they need it, and they are as accustomed to it as they are to flies and [gnats], even in vinegar. Al-Razi <note>Rhazes, the famous Persian physician (865–925 AD)</note> said in his *Book of Causes*: "The meaning of a wound's medicine is its healing."

<margin>Testing the eggs</margin>
**Agrimony** <note>original: "الغافث" - Agrimonia eupatoria</note>: In the context of Arugula, there are three types: *Shayizfan*, *Awfaqan*, and a second reading. The strongest is the natural one; it is bitter in shape. Germander is the one that unites them, and one of its most famous features is its green beauty.

**Castoreum** <note>original: "جندبادستر" - a yellowish secretion from the scent glands of the North American and European Beaver</note>
In the fourth [degree], it is the strongest purgative for chronic [ailments]. It warms the stomach. It is mixed into medicines to counter the "water" that appears in wounds. For Arugula, it is given to those bitten by a rabid dog, as it is the most beneficial and potent shield for them. If the [toxins] are expelled, the patient recovers from the diseases that Arugula [treats]. It was mentioned by Rhazes in the context of Wormwood <margin>Stomach Purge</margin>. It is a bitter poison for the libido, meant to provide purity when medicines indicate a poisoned temperament. No pain shall harm the one who is purified by it. He said: "Whoever is named in the state of leadership..." <note>text trails off or becomes metaphorical</note>.

**Pumpkin seeds** <note>original: "حب القرع"</note> expel [parasitic] seeds from the stomach and are beneficial for colic, sciatica, and hip pain when drunk with honey-water. As for the pulp, it eases the black bile humors, hot winds, and types of semi-paralysis. In general, it is the ultimate goal in the standard treatment for paralysis. Applying a seal of pomegranate [juice] on bitter pumpkin seeds with rosewater and fennel is used for ophthalmia <note>eye inflammation</note>; it cools, strengthens, and prevents skin spots and blisters. ### The Letter Jeem
<margin>In Greek: <unclear>Euzomon</unclear> <note>original: "مواو واحي" - likely a corruption of the Greek name for arugula</note></margin>
**Arugula** <note>original: "الجرجير" (Eruca sativa)</note> is a well-known plant, hot in the third degree and moist in the second. It sharpens the libido, stimulates desire, and increases semen and milk, though it causes gas in the stomach. In the branches of the "Mughlabi" variety are four vessels <note>likely seed pods</note>. When eaten, it strengthens and purifies the skin of freckles. Its benefit is found in drinking its juice up to eight ounces with vinegar or sal ammoniac. We note that it expels great waste—meaning it agitates the spirits so that sweat emerges, thus causing no harm to the limbs; it even expels [toxins] through its path. A drink of one and a half cups of its extract is useful for certain illnesses. A woman with a [uterine] ailment may use it as a pessary before intercourse for several consecutive days to expel it; the sign of its expulsion is finding it solidified. It clears the semen, sharpens the "light" in the stomach <note>digestive fire</note>, cools rashes and freckles, and its flower's potency is like that of celery. It blooms for many days. If four *dirhams* <note>a unit of weight, approx. 3.2 grams</note> of it are taken for ten nights, it heals mange and tested sores. It also helps with [kidney] stones.

### As for the Coconut
<margin>For the Coconut</margin>
It is called *Duruwayh* <note>original: "دورويه"</note> or *Nareel* <note>original: "الناريل"</note>. It is hard and has a bright, flower-like pulp. There are two types: fresh and dry. Its outer shell is fibrous. Its pulp would be bitter if [left too long]. It protects the gums, making them firmer than *Zanzalu* <note>unclear reference, possibly a hard wood</note>, and it strengthens against chronic fevers. It has another story: its [tree] height is four cubits, and at its top, it resembles the head of an owl. It has hard edges like the bulb of the plant called *Melilotus* <note>original: "مليلويس" - Sweet Clover</note>. The coconut serves the purpose of many medicines. Galen mentioned its leaves for joint pain, noting they resemble the root of the marshmallow plant or small Berberis. Its power is long-lasting; the flowers are gathered and used to benefit the joints.

<column-break/>

<margin>**Black Nightshade** <note>original: "عنب الثعلب" (Solanum nigrum)</note></margin>
It is found in abundance in Ethiopia, where the plants grow large. There is another small type with many thorns and small leaves with drooping branches; I saw most of this type growing in the land of the Hijaz. One of our companions asked me about its use for scorpion stings; he said it should be crushed and applied to the sting immediately. It is best for those who suffer from darkness [of vision]. Its leaves are found in abundance in Cairo and in the gardens of the Maghreb <note>North Africa</note> where the *Salsan* grows. It lives for many months and reaches the size of a walnut. It has a fruit from which <margin>**Hemorrhoids**</margin> a treatment for hemorrhoids is derived; it causes them to inflame and then drop off, which is a proven method. It is also mentioned for those who suffer from [unclear] and the atmosphere is heavy. <margin>**The Other Side**</margin> On the other hand, if fried in oil and dropped into the ear, it calms the pain of the vertebrae. Then there is the "Apple of the Cities," which is used to wrap apples in a leathery skin of various types.

### The Letter Jeem
**Germar** <note>original: "جرمار"</note> is the "son of the donkey's scent." In origin, it is the common Germar, called *Moloia* <note>original: "مولويا"</note> in Greek. It is well known and called *Samadhar Abrajia* by the Antonines. There are two types: one has flowers like mallow and wild plants, with a light like the light of the *Daydamin* <note>unclear botanical term</note>, used to drink for ulcers and "fire-sores" <note>burns</note>. Its scent is not like pomegranate, and its size is like a tenth-part branch. The second type is "parallel," called *Ka-samina* in Persian. It is simple and has small heads. In the Roman lands, it is called *Balyum*.

### Germander
<margin>**Germander**</margin>
**Germander** <note>original: "جعدة" (Teucrium)</note> is what is called *Khala-la* in the Nubian language, and its name in Greek is *Pasana* from *Marwa*. Some people understand it to be non-lethal. From its ends, many branches emerge; its leaves are white, and its heads are dark blue. From the white earthy heads, a reddish substance is extracted. The seeds are bitter and are the part used; they are extracted through a parching process.

### Galen
**Galen** says: Germander has a potent, sharp power, hot in the third degree. Therefore, it cuts through thick, viscous humors and expels what is in the urine. It is administered with honey-water, wine, or fennel water for fevers. <margin>**Cuts the difficult**</margin> Some people call it *Germar*, others call it *Samama*. It provides a great cure, similar to the plant called *Moly* <note>a mythical or real herb mentioned by Homer and Galen</note> if its root is white. It grows in the fortresses of many lands.

### The Second Type: Cress Seed
<note>original: "بزر الحرف" (Bazar al-Harf) – Garden Cress seed, known in medieval medicine for its intense "heating" properties similar to mustard.</note>

As for the second of the two types of its seed, it is a species from a sparse tree called *Harmalah* <note>original: "حرملة" - likely referring to a variety of wild rue or a cress-like shrub</note>. Abu Hanifa <note>referring to Abu Hanifa al-Dinawari, a famous 9th-century botanist</note> said, through Ibn al-Farra, that the cress-plant is a tree with slender, reed-like branches. From it, the "cloud-clearer" <note>likely a poetic or local name for a specific bloom</note> emerges; it has many seeds and its leaves are better than walnuts. Dogs leave the seeds until the day they are needed. It is used to treat exits, laurel, and it is taken to the end of a strike or mud that has occurred. It is boiled until it is clear and its [impurities] are gone, then it is left for ten days until it is drunk as a potent draft. Cress causes intense itching and a burning sensation in the throat, being of the utmost heat; it is tested with fire in its form.

<margin>A severe skin rash or cress plant</margin>

Abu Hanifa said regarding cress: it is the grain used for medication, and its varieties include the "unseen" and the "boiled." As for the second type, Muhammad ibn Amrun says the *Fu'lyana* is the cress that possesses a special quality. The *Fu'lyana* is beneficial for the womb and is attributed to it as if it "weeps" with a salty discharge. Cress is harvested in summer; one variety has thin, many-layered leaves, while another has leaves resembling a circle <note>original: "الاستدارة" - roundness</note> but smaller. The finest we have seen comes from the lands called *Tajliyos* <note>likely a corruption of a Greek geographical name</note> in the region of Qubad. The potency of cress seed is sharp and burning, much like mustard seed or the "External" variety.

<margin>Colic</margin>

It is used to treat the pains of the hip known as "the disease of women" <note>original: "النساء" (Al-Nasa) - Sciatica, often called "irq al-nasa" in Arabic medicine</note>, as well as headaches and all diseases that require heating, just as mustard seed provides heat. Mustard seed may also be mixed with water and used as a poultice in the beginning of tumors, but if it is not used [correctly], it is known that it disperses thick humors.

<margin>It acts strongly through the seed</margin>

It acts with great effort, just as mustard seed does, for it resembles it in its path and action. The cress plant itself, if dried, has a potency equal to its seeds. However, as long as it is fresh and not dried, it possesses an inherent moisture. Therefore, the power of these seeds is great. It is categorized as having a low frequency of action when eaten alone with bread; its potency in terms of heat and dryness is at the end of the third degree and the beginning of the fourth <note>In the Galenic system, the 4th degree is the most intense, often reaching the level of being "burning" or toxic</note>. It acts as a powerful diuretic and promotes menstruation.

<margin>Cress seed</margin>

It is good for the stomach, softens the bowels, expels worms, and stimulates swellings of the spleen. It opens blockages and stirs the desire for sexual intercourse. It is found dissolved as "poured cress" or "pasture cress." If it is taken with pure honey, it treats swelling of the spleen and cleanses the ulcers known as *Al-Shahid* <note>original: "الشهيد" - a type of malignant or spreading sore</note>. In its entirety, it expels waste from the lungs.

<margin>Heals quickly</margin>

When cress is eaten, it repels the flow of humors and dries them out. If it is applied to a site...

<column-break/>

<page-num>72</page-num>

<margin>And it cuts away the "Fire of the Persians"</margin>

...where there is an abundance of humors, it dries them and prevents hair loss. It removes the "Fire of the Persians" <note>original: "نار فارسي" (Nar Farsi) - historically refers to shingles, erysipelas, or cutaneous anthrax</note> and its suppuration. When mixed with lime and applied with henna and salt, it ripens white tumors.

<margin>The Hadhu</margin> <note>Perhaps referring to a specific application or a corruption of a botanical name</note>

It also performs this action. When a poultice is made of this seed with mustard and cress, it pierces, cuts, and strips away phlegmatic moisture that reaches the bladder or the kidneys. It acts as a powerful abortifacient, killing the fetus whether it is drunk or used as a suppository. It can be harsh on the stomach. It is stated in the Book of Medicines that it has a special property in removing and expelling bad humors. In the Persian [tradition], it draws pus from wounds and drains the fluid.

<margin>In the eye</margin>

It cleanses the eye of ophthalmia <note>original: "الرمد" - conjunctivitis or inflammation</note>; it dissolves it if diluted and applied as a treatment. It transforms what has become dry and crusty.

<margin>From its water specifically</margin>

Specifically, if its juice is drunk with hot water, it relieves colic and expels harmful worms. Its leaves are bad for the stomach if their juice is drunk [raw]. If five *dirhams* <note>a unit of weight, approx. 3 grams</note> of it are drunk with water, it treats chronic diseases and clears trapped wind (gas) from the body, and it repels the pain of colic.

<margin>Binding the nature</margin> <note>original: "عقل الطبيعة" - a medical term for treating diarrhea or constipation of the bowels</note>

If it is taken roasted, it binds the bowels. If the blood is thin, it thickens it through boiling. Cress seed stimulates a cold liver and excites the kidneys if they are cold. If it is taken for a disease, it is taken roasted with walnuts and red rhubarb. After ten days, if five liters of it are drunk, it cures the general cough and hoarseness and benefits those with a "loose" throat.

<margin>Malignant ulcers</margin>

If it is applied as a poultice on malignant ulcers, it benefits them. If the head is washed with its water, it cleanses it of dirt and viscous moisture and prevents hair loss. It is similar to a type of *Qadi* <note>unclear botanical reference</note>.

<margin>Pustules</margin>

If applied to pustules, it ripens them and benefits the skin. It is also used for scrofula <note>original: "خناقير" - swelling of the lymph nodes</note>. It should be applied to the site gently. When cress is mixed with oil and applied thinly, it benefits difficult and light-sensitive sores of the head, such as favus <note>original: "خزاز" - a fungal infection of the scalp</note>. If eaten with laurel and placed on the "circling pain" <note>likely referring to a type of radiating nerve pain or shingles</note> arising from the spirit, it provides a remedy. If mixed with honey, it relieves the reactions caused by thick humors and repels the pain of the forehead caused by an excess of these humors. When mixed with honey or egg yolks, it treats the remnants of a strike or a fall, or the effusion of a fluid from one limb to another. In whatever way it is handled, it is beneficial. If mixed with roasted [seeds]...

### Al-Qarkajas
<note>original: "القركجس" (al-Qarkajas) – likely a corruption of the Greek *Karkinōdes*, often identified with varieties of Polygonum or sometimes Nettle-leaved plants.</note>
According to **Al-Razi** <note>Rhazes (865–925 CE), the celebrated Persian polymath and physician</note>, it should be called "eye-inflammation herb" in pharmacy. It is close to the variety with long, serrated leaves like a saw, though this is larger. It has a single jointed stalk. It is bitter and beneficial for the relaxation of the stomach, the womb, and for lethargy. In truth, it is the variety known as "hops" <note>original: "الحمل" (al-hummul)</note>, which resembles the garden <term>Lamium</term> <note>original: "المصص" (al-masas) – Dead-nettle</note>, except it is dust-colored. Its stalk and leaves are like those of the Dead-nettle. Some varieties consist of grass that folds over itself. It can be cooked with food or eaten raw; it is restorative for the stomach, cleanses the liver, and matures thick <term>humors</term> <note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance was thought to determine health</note> found between the organs. It prevents food from spoiling and sweetens the breath. In the language of the Arabs, it is similar to the "oil-press" herb.

### Glasswort
<note>original: "حشيشه الزجاج" (Hashishat al-Zujaj) – known in English as Pellitory-of-the-wall (*Parietaria officinalis*).</note>
In the Romance language, it is called *Elxine* <note>original: "الكس" (alks)</note>, and the common people of Al-Andalus specifically call it *al-khuthaytha*. It is also named the "Wild Basil" <note>original: "البادروج" (al-badruj)</note>.

<margin>
It is named Wild Basil, and in the Andalusian dialect, it is called "Daughter of the Wind" <note>original: "بنت الريح" (bint al-rih)</note>. It sometimes grows quite large.
</margin>

In truth, it is also called "Scorpion Herb." Its leaf is of the fourth nerve-type. The plant grows on walls, near drainage pipes, and on stone fences. It has reddish stalks and leaves similar to the plant called <term>Lithospermum</term> <note>original: "ليترس" – likely Gromwell</note>, covered in fine down. The stalks have a rough texture that causes them to stick to clothing. It possesses a cooling power. For "night blindness" <note>original: "العشا" (al-'asha)</note>, its potency is like that of the "water of the tongue," having a cleansing and astringent effect. It grows in moist, cold places and is used to soothe <term>catarrh</term> <note>original: "نزلات" (nazalat) – excessive mucus or discharge</note> and to repel all types of swellings, as is common in household use for breathing issues and acute inflammations. It is also applied to soft, fleshy swellings to dissolve them. Its branches are used in an ointment with rose oil for earaches. It treats "hot sweetness" <note>original: "الحلاوة حارة" – possibly referring to mumps or inflammatory skin eruptions</note> in the skin, and some people use it specifically for mumps. Among the herbs, its dried form is used in measured doses for chronic conditions. From experience, it has a cleansing power due to its action on glass vessels, just like its leaves. Together with rose oil, it has a cooling and astringent power for swellings of the testicles, for cleansing wounds, and for protruding hemorrhoids of the anus. It treats fire burns and the swellings known as <term>qawhala</term> <note>likely a localized term for a type of gastric ulcer or pustule</note> in the stomach and liver, as well as hot and phlegmatic swellings. The juice of the plant, when mixed with <term>ceruse</term> <note>white lead</note> or lead—as will be explained in the section on mixtures—is effective. There are two types of this plant found in the hills and plains. One type, the *al-khuthaytha*, is used for its parts. Then another type of *al-qafum* <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek name like *Epithymum*</note> is distilled; its water is not just a juice but is also beneficial for the eye. It is dropped into the eye to treat swellings of the tonsils, and when mixed with rose oil and ground, it acts as a sedative for pain and for the vessel of the plant.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The sharp/acrid one.
</margin>

The observer will find the head of the plant differs from the "marshmallow" type <note>original: "الختانية" (al-khataniyya)</note>. It is known as the "Eighth of the Poisons" by name, as arranged by **Gist** <note>original: "جسط" (JST) – possibly a corruption of a Greek physician's name like Oribasius or a specific botanical author</note> for its fame throughout the Maghreb. Although it is not firmly classified, it is settled in the "fourth position" as a wild variety growing in ruins. It is recognized by its fruit. Its leaf is similar to the leaf of **Purslane** <note>original: "البعلة الحمقا" (al-baqla al-hamqa) – "The Foolish Herb," so named because it grows in paths where it is stepped on</note>, but it is smaller. It has stalks that spread out across the ground, and the leaves are densely packed together. There is another variety that grows by rivers; its stalks are doubled on the ground, with a rough appearance and broad leaves. It has long stalks between the leaves, and the stem is square. At the top, it is dark, and at the lip of this branch, it gathers black, triangular seeds. The fruit is hard, resembling the "Sea-Horehound" <note>original: "الجنب الحرج السوس" – likely *Sideritis* or a similar labiate</note>. The juice of the plant is composed of a moist essence and a dry, earthy one; its dryness is not extreme.

<margin>
Its taste is sharp/stinging.
</margin>

Despite this, it is heating. It is applied to the body for the fatty tumors that grow in the walls of the skin.

<margin>
Its plant is tested for coldness despite the heat of its water. It is known by the names "Chicken's Foot" <note>original: "رجل الدجاج" (rijl al-dajaj) – likely Fumitory or a type of Knotgrass</note>.
</margin>

The juice of the variety that grows in walls is superior. Both types are suitable for treating hot swellings, wounds, ulcers, and "connecting blood" <note>possibly referring to staunching hemorrhage</note>. It is applied to any place that has a discharge. As for malignant ulcers, if it is applied, it heals the body. It is mixed with lime but should not be left to the point of causing a burn. It treats jaundice and is used for acute swellings. <margin>For rashes and leprosy, use with salmon water and rose seeds.</margin> It treats infections occurring in the mouth, swellings of the throat muscles, and gum pain. The juice of the plant is also used in <term>clysters</term> <note>original: "المحال" – enemas</note>.

<margin>
Used for the "thorn" catheter, seeds, fleshy swellings, and worms in the wild variety.
</margin>

If a measured dose of the green variety is taken, it is effective against worms. When drunk with wine, it acts as an antidote to deadly poisons. Its truth is that it is an "earthy medicine" requiring care in its use. It kills the "twelve-honey" worms <note>likely a reference to a specific type of intestinal parasite like tapeworms</note> called *kartous* and the bitterness called *marafi*. All parts of the plant are used while fresh. It is used for a type of heart pain and drunk for bladder pain and urinary suppression. Both varieties treat colic. Its seeds and flowers, whether fresh or otherwise, are used. The juice of both types is used for the flesh <note>possibly meaning muscle tissue</note>. There is a variety called the "Prickly Poppies" <note>original: "خسكاثية" (khaskathiyya)</note> which is thorny. If the small yellow seeds, which closely resemble fenugreek, are taken while fresh, they benefit those suffering from **stones** generated in the kidneys and bladder. This is especially true of the first variety when drunk.

Original Verjuice <note>original: "al-hisrim" – juice from unripe grapes</note> and its potency for treating ulcers is of the second degree, and for mites <note>original: "al-susa" – likely referring to scabies or skin-boring parasites</note> of the third degree. **Galen** states that the potency of verjuice juice is a commendable strength of the third degree. It is also used for heart palpitations caused by thin, irritating moisture at the mouth of the stomach. Regarding eye salves <term>kohl</term>, it is used today for roughness of the eye, "eating of the lids" <note>blepharitis</note>, and mouth sores. When the fruit is near autumn, it stops bleeding. When used, it should be stirred and pounded until it saturates, then dried and used with a small amount of fat. It is said to benefit those with epilepsy. This wine needs to age for many years to become most effective for many ailments. As for verjuice wine itself, it is prepared by taking the juice before it matures, exposing it to the sun for three days, then pressing it and taking three parts of its juice...

### Stonecrop
**Dioscorides** states in his fourth book that *Marukhia* <note>original: "marukhya" – identifying with Pellitory or a variety of Stonecrop</note> is a small herb resembling the plant called *Asplenium* <note>Spleenwort</note>, though its branches and leaves are more numerous. It grows in the rocks. In practice, it heals "cankers" and the ulcers known as "corrosive." **Galen** <margin>treatment</margin> says in his eighth book that it treats corrosive and eruptive conditions because it heals the ailment called by that name, as well as the swelling occurring at the base of the nails known as *trachys* <note>paronychia or whitlow</note>. According to **Dioscorides**, it is called "the moist, pulling herb" for these nail conditions. Its potency is cooling <margin>varieties</margin> and it dries without irritation, treating bad scars and hot, stagnant tumors. **Galen** says in the seventh book that its known power is its ability to draw out hot matter by preventing the flow <margin>this type of herb mentioned</margin> that hardens and dries in the second degree, much like "bead-water" does, and all things that are naturally cooling.

**Jaza Jalu** <note>original: "جزا جلو" – likely a transcription of a Persian or Greek botanical name, possibly referring to a type of climbing ivy or bryony</note> : Also known as *Ahamda*, it is a tree that resembles vine plants and climbs upon other trees. ### The Fourth Treatise: Aizoon
<margin>The Title</margin> (The Pillar). The meaning of **Aizoon** is "The Ever-living," and it is so named because it does not shed its leaves. It is a type of protective plant, and we shall provide two large chapters on it. It grows most frequently on the clouds <note>likely meaning high altitudes or rooftops</note> of our houses from its growth habit. It is also called *Sisig-hu*. There is a type that smells of **Rue** <note>original: "al-sadhab"; a bitter medicinal herb</note>, used by women, which is called *Harāsās*. It has leaves containing moisture, and it grows in a circular fashion in all states. Its varieties are well-known for their resemblance to **Leeks** <note>original: "al-kurrat"</note>. 

The best of these plants is that which is upright, while the thicker varieties are useful for those with eye ailments. Some are used for eye surgeries to prevent inflammation. Some grow in the mountains. Its strength is restorative. When prepared and tested, and combined with **stewed meat** <note>original: "al-tanjim"; likely a preservation or slow-cooking method</note>, it treats inflammation, beloved ulcers, and **acute swellings** occurring in the eye, as well as wounds to the head and the horse <note>unclear: may refer to veterinary use or a specific type of wound</note>. Its juice is mixed with **rose oil** and applied to **fistulas** <note>original: "al-nawasir"</note> to cleanse and heal them. It is also a cure for the bite of a **Phalangium** <note>original: "al-fawna"; a type of venomous spider</note>. For those suffering from intestinal ailments or ulcers, if it is drunk with wine, it expels **parasitic worms** from the belly and treats **pleurisy** <note>original: "adwa' al-janb"; pain in the side/ribs</note>.
<margin>By it, fluids are drained</margin> It effectively drains the fluids that have become turbid from wind; washing with **honey** is beneficial for this. 

As for the **Small Aizoon**, it resembles the spherical *al-Mahāzīsh* <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek plant name</note>, and it is found among pebbles and stony ground. It has small branches emerging from a single root, numerous and full of round leaves that are somewhat thick and moist when pressed by the hand, attracting students of medicine. It has stalks at the head like those of the **Quraish** <note>likely a local plant comparison</note>, topped with a crown. The strength of this plant's water is the same as the first type. **Galen** <note>original: "Jalinos"</note> mentions it in the seventh book, and the second type is *Sub-hā*. The **Ever-living** and the Small type both excel in their combined properties. It is unlikely that another type will be found, except by those who are specialized, for the people of **Macedonia** <note>original: "al-manin fima kash mriya"</note> believe they have inherited certain knowledge of it. They classify it in the third degree of potency.
<margin>This is one of the degrees of the Horned Plant. It is used for the tumor known as *al-jumma* and swellings occurring from the skull, and tumors that spread and are dried by the hands.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>The Jaundice Plant</margin> **The Jaundice Plant** <note>likely *Chelidonium majus*, or Greater Celandine</note> is a small plant with a round head and three layers in terms of its action. Some people call it the "Five-leafed Herb" <note>original: "baqlat khama yarina"; from Greek *pentaphyllon*</note>, and others call it *Kinariyo*. As for its scent, it is called "The Final One." It is found on the mountain of knowledge. Its leaf is similar to the leaf of **Purslane** <note>original: "al-baqla al-hamqa'"</note>, covered in fuzz. The water of this plant is beneficial because of its strong, hot, and astringent power, which brings joy to the soul. If applied as a poultice with **old figs**, it dissolves **scrofula** <note>original: "al-khanazir"; swollen lymph nodes in the neck</note>.

<margin>The Ground Pine Plant</margin> # # # # **Ground Pine** <note>original: "Khano al-khamr"; from Greek *Chamaepitys*</note>: According to **Dioscorides** in the fourth book, it is a plant with three or four leaves, similar to the leaves of the plant called *Yaghlamus* <note>Greek: *Phlomos* or Verbascum/Mullein</note> or **Reed** leaves, though it is thicker and coarser. It has thorns and a stem like a span in length. Its root resembles a **scorpion’s tail**. It reaches the size of **Horehound**. Some people have cultivated it. We have seen that the juice of this plant, when applied to a **scorpion sting**, provides relief. As for the "Horn of the Good," it is used for slaves <note>unclear: perhaps a reference to common laborers</note> and for **hidden eye ailments** when mixed with **watercress juice**, as well as in enemas, for tumors, scrofula, and jaundice.

<margin>The Horehound Plant</margin> Regarding **Horehound** <note>original: "al-farasiyun"; *Marrubium vulgare*</note>, it kills internal parasites. A small variety of this type is immediately beneficial for the stomach when taken with a bit of ... after being mixed with honey. Its scent is pungent, and its habit is nourishing. It is a necessary cure for the intestines. Horehound is used for many respiratory conditions. It should be used to expel **phlegm**, treat **coughs**, and **bloody expectoration**. Water is extracted from it, and it is known by names such as *Zakariyya*, *Oshiqan*, or *Masis*. It is specifically used for the chest. 

As for its names among the healers: it is put in wine. They understood that it comes from the "covering." If a measure of one and a half **dirhams** <note>a unit of weight, approx. 3 grams</note> is taken and filtered into a vessel, it heals whoever suffers from **heat**, **fever**, and **measles** <note>original: "al-hasba"</note>. It is also good for **smallpox** <note>original: "al-judari"</note> after it has been prepared. Whoever is prone to <term>abdominal rumbling</term> <note>original: "al-karkar"; refers to borborygmus or gas moving in the intestines</note> has a flaccid body and weak strength. As for thick-textured bread, it does not suit one’s diet. Salt-heavy bread and bread that rises quickly are faster to exit the stomach and are less harmful. What harm does exist therein, we have mentioned in our previous words.

As for **barley bread**, it is more effective than wheat bread in purifying the blood and aiding excretion; it generates less gas and has less thick viscosity. Barley bread provides strength, and it is most suitable for those who require a light, immediate nourishment. 

As for <term>ash-baked bread</term> <note>original: "khubz al-milla"; bread cooked directly in hot embers or ashes</note>, it is thicker and stronger than standard bread, harder to excrete, and more acute once digested. As for **chickpea bread**, it remains in the stomach and is not digested quickly. It should be salted and eaten with milk. <meta>This page transitions from the specialized animal-based cures of the previous section (focused on the bat) to the more common botanical and household substances of the medieval pharmacopeia, specifically focusing on the properties and applications of honey and vinegar.</meta>

<margin>For headache</margin>
<margin>For those suffering from dropsy, indigestion, hemorrhoids, cold humors, and phlegm</margin>
**Honey**, even though it is a common substance, can change the temperament of the body's humors <note>original: *mizaj*; the balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> due to its innate nature. When used as nourishment, it is often mixed with ingredients like rose or powders to counteract its potential to generate harmful phlegm. It is applied topically to protrusions or to hard wounds <note>original: *ajs*; likely referring to a hardened mass or tumor</note> to provide relief. A skilled physician uses it when the humor is thick to benefit conditions like dropsy <term>dropsy: an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</term> or indigestion. 

One may also consume a honey-based confection <note>original: *khabis*; a traditional sweet dish</note> on certain days; it was even offered as a gift to treat swelling. If it is poured or spread upon a tumor—whether it is what is called a "longing tumor" <note>original: *fawahmula*; likely a phonetic rendering of a Greek medical term for a specific growth</note> or consumed—or if it is ground and applied as a bandage, it eases pain and the discomfort associated with it. It is also beneficial for the sight; those who wish to improve their vision grind it and apply it to the "darkness of the vision" <note>likely cataracts or dimming vision</note>. It warms the body and helps it gain weight. It may also be used as an antidote to poisons, such as the "deadly khawba" <note>unclear botanical poison</note>, if it is drunk with stone-water. It is particularly effective against the harms of hemlock <note>original: *shukran*</note>. When mixed with a substance called *ufiku* <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek plant name</note>, it becomes a relaxing ointment. If honey is collected from certain trees or mixed with salt, it benefits those who have eaten poisonous mushrooms.

<margin>To remove leeches</margin>
It is also used for those who have swallowed the poison called *yamlas*. As for the "khays," it helps the abdomen when it is afflicted with leeches <note>original: *al-aluq*; leeches were sometimes accidentally swallowed in water, causing internal distress</note> or to ease the lower bowels. 

<margin>Shortness of breath from the lung, spleen, scabies, cough, congestion, and dysentery</term></margin>
It helps with the type of labored breathing that requires the patient to sit upright <term>orthopnea: a condition where one can only breathe comfortably when standing or sitting up</term>. If it is applied as a liniment, it benefits the leaning of a limb toward the side. It is used in cases of "pouring waters" <note>likely pleural effusion or cataracts</note> and croup. When ground, it benefits toothache. Al-Razi mentions in *The Comprehensive Book* <note>original: *Al-Hawi*; the massive medical encyclopedia by the Persian physician Rhazes</note> that vinegar mixed with honey acts against the adherence of leeches. It settles the stomach and cuts through thirst. In the *Book of Regimen* by Al-Razi, it is noted that it extinguishes the heat of fire <note>burns</note> faster than anything else. For those with heart palpitations or a weak lung, the matter is left to clinical judgment. It is not hidden from the one who strikes it; it is a successful generator of "winds" <note>flatulence or gases</note> but aids the appetite and digestion, and cleanses the throat. Hippocrates stated in the *Book of Acute Diseases* that **Vinegar** benefits "cold" organs by cleansing them, though it may transform into a phlegmatic nature. It helps with headaches and conditions of the joints.

<margin>What harms the nerves</margin>
The author of *The Servant's Guide* <note>original: *Sahib al-Khadim*; likely referring to the *Kafi* or a similar manual</note> said that regarding the nerves, clinical experience and analogy show that vinegar—being cold—can cause harm. This is especially true for the roots of the beard because wherever it can reach, it strengthens the penetration.

<column-break/>

It dives deep until it mixes with all parts of the body. **Vinegar** acts similarly against the "blackness" <note>black bile</note> that harms all the nervous organs, such as the brain and others. The second benefit of acidic substances is that if vinegar is used where there is no wound, it is cooling. However, if there is a wound, it may produce a type of heat that turns the area black, much like a burn. Because its powers are compound, vinegar may weaken the natural heat. It is not beneficial for the liver. Al-Fakhr <note>likely the scholar Fakhr al-Din al-Razi</note> said that if it is used as an eye salve while cold, it reduces inflammation.

<margin>The Definition of Vinegar</margin>
Vinegar can weaken the stomach's lining, make the face appear yellow, and weaken the eyesight. It "eats" at the nerves and the stomach's sensitive lining. It cuts through heat and thins the humors. We have found that it is an equalizing substance for the body, both cooling and warming for the organs when poured upon them. If mixed with food and eaten, it benefits "scattered breathing" caused by cold. It is known to benefit the bladder. Al-Razi mentions among its harms that while vinegar suits those of a "yellow bile" and "bloody" temperament <note>choleric and sanguine</note>, it is harmful to those with cold natures. It is said to "boil the meat" and reduce the semen and weaken it. Those who should avoid excessive use of it include those with "thick winds" <note>gas</note> in their stomach and intestines, and women with diseases of the womb. It can affect the color of the skin. Its harms can be corrected by using sweets, especially honey.

<margin>Fever</margin>
Wine and honey return the balance to the body. As for someone who feels food sticking to their liver and is of a hot temperament, vinegar is suitable for them. If the person is of a cold temperament, it should only be used with "hot" medicines like caraway <note>original: *karawya*</note>, onion, and garlic. It should be cooked with these or with legumes and similar things. To mitigate the harm to those with a cough, it should be mixed with sweets, and for those with an angry or sharp disposition, it should be balanced accordingly. Honey is indispensable in meat stews and should be added according to the person's temperament. It purifies the blood and the gall that flows to the mouth. It strengthens the body and expels black bile. Vinegar has a dissolving power and a cutting power <note>original: *quwwa muqatti'a*; refers to the ability to break down thick fluids/humors</note>.

Whoever finds this headache resulting from the consumption of drink should adopt what purifies the thin vapors and eliminates wind. 

As for the preparation of **honey syrup**, one should increase its dilution until it moves away from the potency of wine, and it should be overcome with barley water, or the juice of sour pomegranates, or what is suitable such as roasted grain flour <note>original: *sawiq*; a traditional porridge made from parched barley or wheat</note>. If **quince** is not found, one should place upon the head cooling compresses of rose water and camphor to stop the effects of the drink. One should inhale **rose oil** at bedtime, and supplement it with **violet** and **water lily**, as these are beneficial. 

As for those who turn to **Roman syrups** <note>original: *ashrabat al-rum*; likely referring to imported Byzantine medicinal wines or syrups</note>, they should drink a measure of it, then follow it with **oxymel** <note>original: *sakanjabin*; a medicinal mixture of vinegar and honey or sugar</note> made from vinegar syrup. If the body has consumed it, let him reduce it according to his capacity, or take a sip of sugar. Note that plain, cooled oxymel is less likely to cause the fainting that occurs in the center of the stomach. For those whose liver requires oxymel but finds it difficult to tolerate due to its temperament, they should use a preparation of **sour quince**, clarified and moved to the end of the stomach. Take one part of this and three parts of **plentiful sugar**, then boil it and remove its froth <note>original: *naz'u raghwatihi*; the process of skimming impurities off a boiling liquid</note> until it achieves the proper consistency. One must avoid all types of dregs and heavy sediment. This preparation is similar to others used for the treatment of hoarseness, colic, and the medicinal use of **cheese**, **pomegranate with rose**, and **dried dates**. He intended to hide within it what was strongest. No drink is without some benefit for one day or another, as shall be explained regarding bilious conditions, lentil-based dishes, and stews. In general, avoid all sour pods and gas-producing foods, and one should avoid **onions**, for they harm the senses.

It was mentioned in his saying that the drink should not be taken cold, but rather it should be warmed before being given.
</margin>

...and various types of **cooling foods**. For those who enjoy a certain drink, let it be for the sake of the liver, provided there is no shortness of breath or pain. Rather, it should be used only when the liver is in a state of distress. One must avoid heavy mixtures and cherries, and instead use **preserved celery water** and vinegar. One should include in their diet soups, **pickled truffles**, dill, and <unclear>unripe grapes</unclear>. One must avoid anything that causes a contrary reaction or hastens the hardening of the liver. Avoid sweets especially, particularly those made from **figs** and slow-cooking meats. 

As for those who suffer from liver blockage alongside shortness of breath, they should consider an infusion <note>original: *qahwa*; in this period, it refers to a strong medicinal decoction or wine that suppresses appetite</note> and medications that promote the flow of celery juice and contain much **ginger**, mixed with cold medicines. If there is numbness along with the coldness, treat it with hot water in the bath to dissolve it. One may use a porridge of truffles, even though the use of astringent substances <note>original: *'afs*; gallnuts or similar tannins</note> is known in the treatment of related conditions. 

It has been found through experience that certain drinks are taken out of necessity, even if they are thick. From the types of drinks like those of the *Zamir* people, the physician should choose what is neither thick, nor murky, nor overly sweet. Choose instead that which is clear, slightly bitter, and thin. Adjust its temperament and drink it after the fatigue of a meal, but not upon a completely empty stomach. Some people mix **raisins** from the beginning of the drink's preparation; if they do so, the drink will not overcome the intellect, provided it is consumed with wisdom. 

Excessive consumption requires the prior drinking of **julep** <note>original: *jallab*; a sweet drink made of rose water and sugar</note> and **oak balsam** to correct its viscosity. Then, after every meal, one should delay drinking until the strength of the food has settled. Those who suffer from the "heat of the drink" and pain in the liver—which is recognized by a fever and a heaviness on the right side—should drink a medicated syrup with water. They are harmed by large amounts of water and frequent movement. One should close the wound <note>metaphorical: heal the affliction</note> and consume **almonds**, **walnuts**, and **pistachios**. One should avoid legumes and moist fruits until the "heat" of the stomach subsides. 

As for those who experience from the heat of the drink a loss of appetite, fainting, nausea, and a foul-smelling breath, accompanied by a heavy head and **disturbed sleep**, these are signs of "hot diseases" resulting from wine. This occurs if the wine is burnt <note>cooked down too much</note> or if the person remains in a state of sleep for a long duration.

# Folio 49

Since drink is one of the two components of nourishment, when it is consumed, it is processed and separated by the **innate heat** <note>original: "al-gharizi"; the vital heat believed in medieval medicine to drive digestion and life</note>. If it passes beyond its proper limits, it weakens the strength suddenly, and through it, **heart palpitations** and tremors occur. If the drink is clear, it may be beneficial, but if it is not, one should cease drinking immediately and sleep peacefully.
The <term>Basilic vein</term> <note>original: "al-basliyu"; a major vein in the arm often used in bloodletting</note> should be considered if putrefaction is feared, or if the mixture of humors is such that it cannot be ignored. **lote-tree** <note>original: "sidr"</note>. This should be used every day and is especially beneficial for cases of **hiccups** <note>original: "al-fuwaq"</note>, as is apple water and pomegranate.
<margin>Concerning the membrane of the heart and heart palpitations</margin> This is a noble medicine to strengthen the heart against intense heat; it is suitable for palpitations accompanied by heart tremors and heat. This is prepared from what is ground or infused with **sandalwood** and poplar. 
If the drinking and the subsequent tremors persist, the person should immediately, upon feeling the head move, stop drinking and sleep until the next day. ## Fifth: On the Liver, the Veins, and the Two Sides

In the "Book of Relief" <note>original: "Kitab al-Faraj"; likely a reference to a specific medical text on easing suffering</note>, there is a principle, not just in a specific branch: know that a ringing occurred in its color, nor from one who settled for <unclear>pain</unclear>. The pain starts from its hour; even if it bursts and becomes lighter and firmer, a man might die of the pain, yet it returns the child to strength. Fifthly: as for **smallpox** and pain in the flank, he places him in the exit of a bath where game [animals] gather to block the heaviness and the matter. If its passage is cut, it benefits greatly. This occurs most often in the lungs and the chest. Among them are those who suffer from sorrow and enmity from their youth, and from the muscles. When smallpox is secreted and the painful matter exits in the springtime—as for the material pain, it is the blood of the wounds from the flowing flesh. As for the **hernia**, perhaps it occurred during the state of death. With every helping hand in its springtime, it offers a powerful defense. As for the nature of the lungs, until its strength emerges, it is seen as beneficial for **hemorrhoids**. The oil of the remaining hemorrhoids in the anus is of wondrous benefit. As for a sign from the leeches used to block the pungent [humors], after purification with water, barley water, and a wide leaf, the vein is lowered and **sealed**. 
In the youth, and for those who have drunk of the "meat-tree" <note>original: "lahm al-shajar"; possibly a pulpy plant</note>, whether it be wet or dry or otherwise, there is the fatigue of the negligent among them, not rest. For whoever is overcome by the "gluttonous" <note>original: "al-lawwam"; literally 'the blamer', here perhaps a morbid appetite</note>, his heel, if taken when wild, changes from black and green to white. 
The immersion of the eye in ordinary swelling, meaning it is elongated for him like a "faluz" <note>a sweet starch-based dish; here describing the shape of a swelling</note>, and the evil **colic** or the passing matter. The meat-light overcomes it in the power of attaining unity; whether it was dry or if one drank water or wine, it cuts the colic. 
<margin>Feed him pomegranate seeds with salt and mastic to strengthen the gall bladder.</margin>

### **Dar Shish’an** <note>Likely the Sea Buckthorn or a similar thorny aromatic shrub</note>

This is its name in the common tongue, while in the Berber language of the Sudan it is called *Azward*. It is not used without being mixed. Its identifying marks are that it is a small tree with many branches and a rough outer bark, covered in many thorns. It grows in the lands called *Idhkir*, which are also known as the lands of *Dovina*. Perfumers rely on its branches, and it is prepared by thickening <insert>Azward herb</insert>. Its leaves are evergreen, tending toward black. In Persian, it is called *Abbar Jayba Kabya*, having a pleasant scent and a taste with a hint of bitterness. There is another yellow variety, which is rough and lacks a good scent. The best quality is that which has prominent, visible features and is classified among the types of **Galangal**. Its growth resembles the **Laurel** <note>original: "al-Rand"</note>, except that it has offshoots. It produces a hard, pungent sap with a sharp bite like garlic. Its branches bear delicate leaves, so fine they are hardly visible to the observer. Its fruit is smaller than a plum and has a fragrant aroma. The root is rough and black; this is the part used medicinally. It is also known as "Eye-Spots" <note>indicating its use for cataracts or vision</note>. 

If it is unavailable, its substitute is the roots of **Cassia** or the bark of the **Turnip** plant <note>original: "Lifat"</note>. In the lands of Africa, it is called "Wood of the Prominence" or "The Grieved." It is also called *Habarda*. Women use it on the wedding night as a perfume from the stone, placing it under the pillow of the groom or the prince; it is said that if he sleeps, he will see in his sleep whatever he desires through a frequency of dreams.
<margin>I am familiar with this "Ghafia" <note>lethargy/forgetfulness</note> and the poisons; the Arabs have discussed them in another place.</margin>

**Halsumis** <note>Likely Alyssum, from the Greek 'Alysson'</note>
The potency of this plant is composed of various qualities. It is categorized as being in the new heat, though its airy parts provide a cooling effect, but it is feared for its moisture. It is useful for ulcers that have taken hold in the lower materials. It is similar in potency to **Dar Shish’an**, especially when taken with the peel. It is used in treatments when cooked as a drink, for rinsing the mouth, and for foul ulcers in the mouth or malignant ulcers on the body. It helps expel the fetus if placed in a vaginal suppository. It is also found in the "Sea Woods," having a taste of meat and a scent like black musk. The description of **Dar Shish’an** continues: it is effective in its second degree of potency.

<column-break/>

<margin>The *Munkhasi* Sea Stone, also named "The Fish."</margin>
<margin>This is Cassia, and its potency is hot in the second degree.</margin>

Its specific property is that it extracts "evil sea-matter" from the moisture when used as a collyrium <note>eye medicine</note>. It is recommended to be used with other ingredients. Its root is ground into a fine meal, especially with poppy juice, which is the correct way to apply it. It dissolves "red phlegm" and clears the chest and lungs of the moisture that settles there. It is highly regarded for its cleansing properties...

It is more beneficial than other substances in solidifying moistures due to its virtue in [healing] any organ. It is useful for the disease called "The Heat" and for **Hyssop** <note>original: "Zufa"</note> in warming the liver and gathering excess moistures. It significantly improves the complexion, especially when mixed with **Kafli** <note>a type of lead-based medicinal or pigment</note>. It acts as a dye for the body and is a carminative against wind. It is beneficial for pains of the womb when used as a liniment in its oil form...

It is useful for fistulas. If mixed with **Saffron**, it counters the heaviness of the stomach. It should not be used excessively for the stomach if there is blood present, as it can thicken the humors in the chest. It is not as effective against excessive gas as **Pepper** or **Galangal**. Its excellence is proven when raisins are added to it for dry organs. It has a property that aids breathing through its fragrance and the persistence of its heat. It is used as a juice or a tonic. When prepared with "rectifiers" <note>balancing agents</note>, its water benefits those suffering from ailments descending from the head to the chest and lungs.

**Jasyufon** <note>Likely a transliteration of Xylo-cassia or a Greek botanical name</note>
Mentioned in the books of the Greeks as a variety that equals the weight of **Cinnamon**. The Arabs say its potency is even higher. It dissolves tumors and should be used with other medicines...

As mentioned by **Ibn Abi Anna** in his poetry, there is a variety that appears as dry **Cassia**. The potency of sharp Cassia is close to **Cinnamon**. As for **Ghadani Cinnamon**, it is stronger than the finest Cassia, like the Indian variety. It is necessary to distinguish the scent from other types... and to differentiate it from the "vile Cassia" often found in its place. In any case, its weight is less during the harvest season, and it was used to light fires...

# **Cress** <note>original: "Huruf" – usually referring to Garden Cress, *Lepidium sativum*</note>

It refers to the tips of the plant; the best parts are those that are tender in color, the coarsest among them being the color of a leek. It tends toward redness and has a pungent coarseness. Some people apply it as an ointment made from <unclear>male flies</unclear> <note>original: "dhikru dhubaba" – this may be a transcription error for a specific plant or mineral part</note> without incision. It arrests a cough and helps with pain from green, small, sour varieties. The sixth type is a compound substance consisting of pungent elements, water peach, and others; the smaller it is, the sharper its effect. It is proper for it to be surrounded by a thick peel. Its interior is very pungent, meaning it possesses much heat. Its interior is as pungent as mustard, though its scent is not as sharp. # **Leeches** <note>original: " 'Alaq"</note>

### Ash Tree Seeds

This is the name for **Sparrow’s Tongues** <note>original: "Lisan al-Asafir," the common name for the seeds of the Ash tree (Fraxinus)</note> in Persian. It resembles the "tongue of the morning." It is found in cold regions. One type has two forms of exit: one is rough and bitter, from which the husk can be peeled just as rice is peeled; the other is like sand, sharp with no sweetness. It is of the southern genus, and its appearance is similar to the **Naja** <note>possibly a reference to a specific plant or a "serpentine" shape</note>, and its power is similar to its power. It is used in medications to "grip" the stomach, just as the walnut tree does. As for external use, if its seeds are placed inside flesh, they shrink it. 

The second type is from the group used to make bread, as is done with **Al-Jawzun** by its people; it is warming. Its nature is cold in the first degree and dry in the second degree. It helps with the flow of urine and is beneficial for the bones and the stomach. As for its use in the urethra or for blood and resins, there is no harm in it. It has a trembling effect on its food and is quick to transition in the system. In the "cave" <note>likely referring to a deep-seated ailment or the nasal cavity</note> it benefits epilepsy since it is drying to the layer, as if it were raw. It contains the essence of the earth, and it possesses a purifying quality against the "fire" that burned that substance. As for its essence which used to cause swelling, it is a fine earthy substance. After this, the types of materials are mixed. 

The substance of the sun is a single thing. It is said to be like the heat of the **Liquid Storax** <term>al-mi'ah: a fragrant resin or balsam</term> and the heat of **Frankincense** <term>al-kandur</term>. These are animal-like mixtures for medicines used for the eye or the thinness that has a gap. They treat eye ulcers and prevent the "water" <note>cataracts</note> that forms in the eye and dissolves it. Those who use it as a collyrium <term>kuhl</term> do so because of what they feel of its difficulty and pain. Each of these is very effective. As for the **Liquid Storax**, it is stronger than its water. It has two heats, and I say its heat is like the heat of pitch. Scribes use its water. There are types that are more biting in treating diarrhea, especially when the ailment is a collection of diarrheal symptoms accompanied by "the stranger" <note>likely a foreign matter or an unusual discharge</note>. They are used in treating those discharges and the itching that occurs in the corners of the eye, as well as for treating the "moist eye" <note>tearing or discharge</note> that accompanies it.

# Shish 
It is the plant called *Al-Haym* <note>Oleander</note>, and I have mentioned it previously, but this is the beautiful [variety]. In Greek, it is called *Orengi* <note>original: *orengi*, likely a corruption of *nerion*</note>, and its taste is like that of the vine. Both are small and do not describe the fourth quarter. It is a well-known shrub resembling almond leaves, but it is longer, thicker, and greener. Its flower is similar to the red rose. It bears something like the Syrian carob, which opens in its clusters. 

The wool-workers have their signs in the flower of the plant called *Aphyllanthes* <note>original: *Awafilis*</note>. Another type is the *Khaf-kuda*, which fills the medicine and resembles garden plants in the marshes. The juice of the eighth plant heals the fever of people. If applied to the body externally, it strengthens it. If mixed with bindweed (*lablab*), it is very effective. If a woman in postpartum takes it until blood is discharged, the hand is healed—though they say it causes "soul-expansion" <note>possibly euphoria or a respiratory effect</note> and does not cause constipation, but rather reduces much of the colic. As for its temperament, it is in the second degree of moisture and the third degree of dryness at its limit. 

Among the medicines, it is best not to heat it; it has the power of sight. Eating the plant is fatal to dogs, donkeys, mules, and livestock in general. However, if it is drunk with wine, it saves people from bites and various types of poisons; its specialty is that it clarifies the effect of poisons. <margin>Mountain Cinnamon</margin>
On Cinnamon, Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> teaches that the people consider the best cinnamon to be that which comes from the lands of India. It is known among the people as "Mountain Cinnamon." It consists of thin, long pieces with pipes that are well-aligned and joined together, resembling the *dafi* <note>likely *Daphne* or laurel</note>, though its fragrance is greater and its taste sharper. Today, it is considered superior to the soft, twining variety.

<margin>The Best Cinnamon</margin>
Furthermore, regarding Cinnamon, Dioscorides teaches that the best of these cinnamons has thin, reed-like sticks; its color and its end are pleasant in scent, and it is sharp and bitter to the taste. The qualities of cinnamon are lost if it is yellow. The finest variety of this cinnamon is not merely hot in nature, but of a specific kind; it has a delicate color resembling *ghaliya* <term>ghaliya: a costly medieval perfume blend of musk, ambergris, and oil</term> and its wood possesses the scent of "Royal Leprosy" <note>likely a colorful name for a specific aromatic quality or grade</note>. This high quality occurs because it comes from the wild, possessing a certain bitterness. In scent and potency, cinnamon is very heating and drying; it opens the mouths of the veins, dissolves and moistens, and cuts through thick humors. It is said that when its fragrance is strong, it drives away pains of the uterus <note>original: *al-rahm*</note> if mixed with oil and its essence is thickened. If it is bound and joined together, it can be known to draw and enter deeper than other medicines.

<margin>Good for fistulas</margin>
When mixed with pitch <note>original: *ghira*</note>, it is beneficial for fistulas <term>fistula: a chronic, tunnel-like sore or abnormal connection between organs</term> and for medicines prepared for the stomach, and for the treatment of diseases and sores where the flesh is rotting, and for tumors that appear. When used this way, it acts as a general healer. It also benefits those suffering from anxieties, kidney diseases, and stones, as well as those wandering with stomach pain and physical trauma; it is of great benefit for the strength of such afflictions.

---

### On Spikenard

<margin>Nard</margin>
Dioscorides says regarding Spikenard <note>original: *al-nardeen*, a fragrant Himalayan herb used in ancient perfumes and medicine</note> that there are various types in its preparation. Sometimes it is made into dyes, and sometimes it is drawn out. Most of the bitter varieties are prepared from nard, and from Nabataean nard. It is used because its essence benefits the lungs and those with respiratory depletion. It is seasoned with various liquids. The finest of this nard is that which has thin sticks and a pleasant, sweet scent. The scent of nard is measured by its fragrance and its potency. This nard is warming and "royal," being very hot and corrective. There is also a variety from Tyre, but its scent should not be described as changing. It is prepared in another way, where the nard is drained and the essence is extracted.

<column-break/>

<margin>Made from laurel leaves and oil; heat it for forty-eight days, twice each day</margin>
Take five ounces of *kadi* oil <term>kadi: oil from the screw-pine or Pandanus flower</term> in a wide-shaped flask and place it in hot ground until it ferments with the oil and salt, so that its color and scent return. Then cool it in fine vessels. In the summer, it is used to wash the crown of the head. It is also learned from the people that some take six pounds of oil and five pounds and two ounces of balsam wood. Its strength is extracted by those who mix it with the oil and boil it until the essence rises. From this, nine pounds and some ounces of ... <unclear>abir fak'a</unclear> ... are taken with *andro-stati* <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek botanical term like *androsaces*</note>. From the olive oil, fourteen pounds are taken, and an equal weight of ... <unclear>balqam</unclear> ... is added. If you wish to cool the strength of the taste, it is good to leave it in the oil for a day and a night, repeating this two or three times. Then press it. The strongest of this oil is that which has nothing else added to its scent. This includes what is sent from the wild, which is called "tension bud" and the "philia" variety. From the wild lands called Achaia <note>a region in Greece</note>, it comes in this form. The power of this oil is softening and it follows the steam of the breath; it is a cooling and beneficial remedy.

<margin>Uterine pains, acute tumors, the back, expels the fetus, and opens the mouths of hemorrhoids and fistulas</margin>
It is used for uterine pains, acute tumors, and pains of the back. It expels the fetus and opens the mouths of hemorrhoids and fistulas. If used with vinegar, it is also suitable for the chest.

<margin>Malignant sores</margin>
It is used for malignant sores. The preparation should be cooled to increase its effect. It is beneficial for the liver and heals the uterus and the mouth when used in a bath. It promotes urine and heals hernias. For those whose bodies have become heavy, it nourishes them. It is also helpful for choking and roughness in the windpipe, or for those who have been affected by henbane <note>original: *al-banj*, a toxic plant used as an anesthetic or poison</note> or bad vapors.
