## Fenugreek Oil
A bitter oil is extracted from Fenugreek <note>original: *al-hulba*</note> using a distillation process. Take five *ratls* <term>ratl: a medieval unit of weight roughly equivalent to a pound</term> of olive oil, one *ratl* of "shrubby" reeds <note>likely *Vitex agnus-castus* or a similar aromatic shrub</note>, and two *ratls* and one ounce of the infusion. Keep it in the oil for seven days, stirring it three times each day, then strain it. Some people soak the oil with "Kamduna" water <note>unclear: possibly a regional name for a specific mineral water or plant infusion</note>, then cook it gently with the fenugreek and similar herbs. It has a softening power for abscesses <note>original: *al-dabla*</note> and is suitable for hardness occurring in the uterus. It is used as an enema for a woman's uterus that has become foul-smelling or dry, as it purifies the humors. It is also beneficial for tumors of the rectum and is used for sciatica <note>original: *al-zanjir*, likely a corruption of *al-nisa*</note>. It relieves griping pains, clears dandruff from the head and its wet sores, and makes moles shine. <margin>The bitter [oil] is produced from olive oil and a specific amount of moisture.</margin> <margin>This oil is well-tested and effective for all the conditions we have mentioned.</margin>

## Rue Oil
It is beneficial for pain of the kidneys, bladder, back, and uterus, as well as for nerve relaxation <note>palsy or weakness</note> and pain in the sides. It calms severe pain, dissolves "winds" <note>gas or flatulence in the medieval sense</note>, and treats fistulas <note>original: *al-nasur*</term> if rubbed into them. Half an ounce of it may be used in the bath to cleanse the body of tremors; this is a proven remedy. It helps with all pains in the lower hands and feet, and if dropped into the ears, it benefits "cold" earaches. If used as an enema, it helps with types of colic and intestinal blockages caused by viscous phlegm or thick gases. Its preparation: four and a half *ratls* of oil, four ounces of Rue <note>original: *sadhab*</note>, and five and a half *ratls* of water. Cook it over a gentle fire until the water evaporates and only the oil remains, then cool and strain it. <margin>For cold earaches, gas, fluids, rumbling, and deafness.</margin>

For weakness of the cold, phlegmatic, and bilious brain; for pains, bloating, and cracks.

Al-Tamimi <note>Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Tamimi, a famous 10th-century physician</note> states: smelling it and inhaling it warms a brain of "cold" temperament, strengthens it, dissolves the "winds" present in its nerves, and removes any dryness within. It also repels uterine pains, dissolving cold tumors and inducing menstruation <note>original: *al-tamth*</note> immediately if rubbed onto the areas affected by a phlegmatic temperament or black bile.

## Chamomile Oil
This oil is extracted as moderately hot and is a well-tested remedy. It calms pains and is beneficial for all fevers arising from blood inflammation. It softens hardened joints and benefits all pains occurring in the limbs by dissolving tumors rooted in phlegm, yellow bile, or black bile. The nature of Chamomile <note>original: *babunaj*</note> is such that it is easily made; one can take the small stalks, like a small rod, and strip the flowers or pluck the rose with its light. <margin>In the treatment of the intestines and hot tumors.</margin>

## Narcissus Oil
This oil is extracted by taking six portions of olive oil and placing them in a sealed vessel for three or four [days], along with lamb’s gall. It is buried for eight days and then used in poultices. Some put it in a wide vessel and boil it in a cold or temperate room, covering it with a very thin cloth and leaving it for many days until its color changes. Others wrap it in leather or cloth for fifteen days until the scent of the Narcissus <note>original: *narjis*</note> is thoroughly infused into the oil and matures. Then it is squeezed out. It has an astringent quality and repairs scabby sores, scalp conditions, and "the ant" <term>the ant: *al-namla*, a historical term for spreading skin eruptions like shingles or herpes</term>. It also treats uterine sores; using it as a wash for the uterus is beneficial, and it helps with burning urination if applied to the penis <note>original: *al-dhakar*</note>. It is also effective for those who spit blood, for hot headaches, hot colds <note>coryza</note>, liver tumors, and gout-like diseases originating from the liver. If used as an enema, it provides clear benefit for intestinal sores and relieves belching by breaking up clotted blood. <margin>For sores, especially in the uterus, the penis, and <unclear>urinary</unclear> issues.</margin> <margin>For spitting blood in the chest, for pain, and for liver diseases.</margin>

## Caper Oil
This oil is extracted from Caper flowers <note>original: *al-kabar*</note> and sesame oil, using one and a half *ratls* of each, plus sheep’s fat. It is placed in a vessel in boiling water. It possesses a natural astringent power and acts as a diuretic, God willing. It is an excellent dissolver [of humors], and the best version of this oil is that which is ground. <margin>Dissolves tumors located in the liver and spleen.</margin>

### Mastic

Know that **mastic** <term>mastic: a resin obtained from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus)</term>, as is said, is related to the laurel, though some versions of the text state it is its own tree. It secretes a turquoise-colored substance. This secretion only happens at the end [of the process] from the opening of the tree’s bark. Under the cut, the mastic is gathered to be purified. 
The best mastic is that which is feared to be [too] hard, and its bulbs, when found in all bodies, tend to tighten and soften. It is also suitable for enemas. 
<margin>Colic...</margin>
It strengthens the stomach and its flavor is far superior to other resins. It is also excellent for removing marks on the face and scars on the head, as it has a cleansing weight. From it, an oil is made on the island where it is harvested to prevent stomach weakness. It is applied to other skins [hides]. The measurement is three parts, or as one might take six ounces of mastic and cook it over a gentle fire in a double-pot <note>original: "qidr mada'wa," referring to a bain-marie or double boiler</note> until the mastic melts into the oil. It is then removed from the fire, left to sit, and stored for when it is needed.

### Castor Oil

**Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential Greek physician whose theories dominated medieval medicine</note> says in the sixth [book of his work] that this oil is extracted from **castor** <term>castor: Arabic "al-khirwa'," the source of castor oil</term>, which has seeds resembling the markings on an eye. One should press them by hand to obtain the essence.

### Castor oil is prepared as follows for the benefit of wounds

Take the seeds and pound them after they have been dried, then strain them. Collect what can be taken. Another method is to take the castor beans and place them in a vessel in the sun for days, then use what comes out of them. Some use fire, but that is against the nature of the oil as it burns it. The Egyptians take it in large quantities; they use it for lamps and also place the castor seeds in bread dough and press them with a screw-press <term>screw-press: Arabic "lawlab"</term>. The sign that the oil is ready is when the husk is removed.

### Oil of Wormwood

## Tail of the Carob
<note>Likely *Scorpiurus vermiculatus*, a plant with seed pods that resemble a carob pod or a curled tail.</note>
Abu al-Abbas said, and the scholar Ibn Idris confirmed, that it appears with flowers east of the **Wild Carob** <note>original: "al-sharwa"</note>; as was said regarding the *Bardani* plant, it is the thing most resembling the carob tree among plants, though it is taller. It is the crown of the plant called in Greek **Stachydion** <note>original: "Stachys"</note>. It shares characteristics in its fruit, seeds, and leaves, and what is associated with the male and the "blue" variety, which is the **Indigo** <note>original: "al-niliyya"</note>. Others have mentioned it elsewhere; some of its leaves are in the "third degree" <note>Medieval medicine ranked potency from 1 to 4; the 3rd degree indicates a very strong effect</note> of medicinal power. It was called the "Tail of the Carob" due to an error by the people of Africa [Ifriqiya]. There is another plant called "Black Water of the Reed," its description and qualities are found in other places; it tends toward bitterness and is distinguished by a stickiness in its leaves. It resembles the plants found commonly in Al-Andalus [Spain] in its safety. Regarding the **Leontice** <note>original: "Labruni"</note>, one must think of its effect on the limbs as slightly drying in its half-state. Its shape is like a carob with seeds like **Caraway** in its roots. It has seeds, and experience has shown their potency against **scorpion venom**, specifically its juice and seeds. I saw it in the lands of Egypt—may God Almighty protect us—and here as well, this "Carob," which is a magnificent tree of its kind.

## The Rabid Dog and the Mouse’s Tail

It is **Plantain** <note>original: "Lisan al-Hamal," literally "Lamb’s Tongue"</note> and is also called *Badhar-lab*. There is nothing like it in its nobility and quality. It contains seeds the size of **Caraway**. It is cold for the liver... in the opinion of Galen in his *Book of Humors* <note>original: "Kitab al-Kammus," likely referring to the *Book of Chymes*</note>. Its plant-water is pleasant in appearance and benefit. It is preferred for the mouth and for those seeking recovery from its pains. Because its roots are small, they are often covered.

# The Varieties and Nature of Rhubarb

It is smooth, topped with a yellowness tinged with a bit of blue. Some people say it is the root of the "Black Agran" called *al-Hajrūnah*. In its essence, some people have delayed <unclear>recognizing it</unclear>, as it appears with a white color like a frightening almond from <unclear>Sifasa</unclear> when their "livers" are scooped out. It is also sometimes called Indian Rhubarb. From the seventh <note>likely referring to the seventh book of a medical compendium</note> of those who discuss it, mention is made of **Turkish Rhubarb**, which is thought to be related to it, and some travelers take it for themselves.

**As for** the Rhubarb that **Galen** did not mention in the *Therapeutics* nor in his book *On Simple Medicines*, although practitioners today give it high regard, it is essentially <note>original: "Atārid," possibly a corruption of a Greek name or a specific merchant's name</note> who brings the "Zanjī" variety of Rhubarb while it is still fresh in its growing place. Its nature is locked within the body of the Rhubarb itself without being transferred into any other substance. Whatever is taken from filtered juice and thickened by fire is considered **adulterated**. This type of fraud is committed so that the Rhubarb retains its form, dries out, and can be sold as if its juices had not been extracted, all out of a desire for profit. <margin>Known as *al-Khaswah* <note>literally "the testicle," likely referring to the shape of the root nodules</note></margin>

**Regarding** its general and specific actions: since the three types of Rhubarb—known as **Chinese**, **Zanjī** <note>East African or "Black" variety</note>, and **Barbi**—are similar in their actions and powers, they only differ in minor increases or decreases. Since Chinese Rhubarb is superior to the others, I have chosen to treat them as one topic, noting the specific case of each variety as I repeat the most potent qualities. 

The nature of Rhubarb is dictated by two specific properties known to us: it is "constricting" and "pungent," composed of different elements. In the expert opinion, it is a balanced substance that stimulates the fetus <note>or "innate heat"</note>. It is said to have a cold, dry, earthy essence, yet it also contains heat because it is composed of a hot, fiery essence that is subtle and airy. Its bitterness indicates a cleansing action, though its effects also arise from its secondary qualities such as weight, softness, and brittleness, which indicate its strength. The best variety is that which possesses these traits; such a plant is filled with life-force, primarily clean in substance, and clearly hot and dry in temperament. It is evident that its powers are far superior to the average medicine. 

Rhubarb's actions, both general and specific, are as follows: first, it acts by squeezing and "squaring" <note>original: "al-tarbī'", likely meaning to balance or structure</note> the thick, viscous fluids of the body and expelling them. Secondly, it acts by dissolving and thinning, as in the case of **swellings** <term>Awrām</term> and thick **gases** <term>Riyāh</term>. It also opens blockages, cleanses, and purifies.

<column-break/>

<margin>The stomach, the liver, and the humors</margin>
<margin>Stimulates urine</margin>
<margin>Hiccups and flatulence</margin>
<margin>For wind, bloating, fatigue, and colic caused by coldness; and for "hardness" in the liver and stomach</margin>
<margin>Medicines and drugs</margin>
<margin>Hellebore <note>original: "al-Khirbaq"</note></margin>

It cleanses the channels and the **lymphatic vessels** <note>original: "al-mafāwī", referring to the body's internal drainage pathways</note>, and acts as a diuretic and an emmenagogue <note>stimulates menstrual flow</note>. It prevents materials from putrefying and strengthens relaxed organs. It hardens moist, neglected ulcers. 

Since its most prominent properties are its medicinal powers, even if there is a hot swelling, it may resolve it because its types of actions are diverse. Its "hot essence" descends and dissolves, while the "earthy essence" stabilizes and reaches the site of the ailment. It performs its actions through its specific power of opening blockages and purging the remnants of poisons from swellings. Some say that in Rhubarb there is a "repelling power" that cools, but its "constricting power" is not as strong as a gargle, nor is it used for the type of surgery that arises from cauterization. 

I have researched its use, especially in internal diseases, regarding what it clears of thin humors—as some of the ignorant commoners think. However, it is clear that it purifies the body of various types of humors and disperses their vapors until they reach the exit points.

**As for** its specific actions: Rhubarb as a whole is beneficial for the liver, the stomach (even a dry stomach), the kidneys, the bladder, and the uterus. It is a powerful strengthener that opens their blockages and lightens deep-seated pains. It brings down the heat of disease and "heavy" fluids, and it dissolves wind. Therefore, it is very effective for those with a "thick" temperament. 

When there is excess matter in the stomach or liver, it is a "medicine of the flesh," especially for mixed humors. It is used for **Dropsy** <term>Istisqā'</term> <note>edema or fluid retention</note> arising from a hot swelling in the liver, and for **Jaundice** <term>al-Barqān</term> <note>likely an OCR variant of 'al-Yaraqān'</note> caused by liver obstructions. 

When added to other medicines and drugs—such as **Aleppo Scammony** <note>original: "al-Shibl al-Halabī"</note>, or **Hellebore** <note>original: "al-Khirbaq"</note>, or others—it is specifically used for the needs of the spleen and for calming pains, especially cold obstructions or "heavy" hiccups and fatigue. It treats colic when taken in **Basil-scented wine** <term>Sharāb al-Rayhānī</term> with camphor water. If the person has ulcers, we find it is beneficial for the stomach and bloating in many ways. It can be taken alone or with "Syrup of Roses" made from dried roses. It is most effective and evident in its specialty for the stomach and the liver—and particularly the liver.

<margin>
Most people believe that blue vitriol <note>original: "al-qalqant"; from the Greek *khalkanthos*, copper sulfate</note> is "elephant’s breath," and in ancient times it was called "the spirit of blue vitriol." In reality, it is a mineral. **Galen** <note>original: "Jālīnūs"; a prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire (129–c. 216 AD)</note> noted in the margin that blue vitriol is the same as white vitriol <note>original: "al-qalqadīs"; likely zinc sulfate or a pale grade of copper vitriol</note>. In summary, the name "blue vitriol" is applied both to white vitriol and the green vitriol <note>original: "al-zāj al-akhḍar"</note> known in Greek as *khalkanthos* <note>original: "khsantiq"; a corruption of the Greek *khalkanthos*</note>.
</margin>

### Book Fourteen: Honor

As for **Dragon’s Saliva** <note>original: "rīq al-tinnīn"; likely referring to "Dragon's Blood" resin or a specific mineral exudate</note>, if it is taken fresh and applied to wounds, it preserves and heals them. There are also the pipes of lead <note>original: "al-raṣāṣ"; often used in the production of medicinal oxides</note> from which a treatment for pustules and fractures is made. In his time, [the author] disliked the uses of each type of vitriol-spit: the "noble white" vitriol—called *arsenikon* <note>original: "irsīn"; likely a corruption of the Greek for arsenic-bearing or a specific vitriol grade</note> in Greek—as well as the thick and the fermented types, and those known as *melanteria* <note>original: "falfantas"</note>, *chalkitis* <note>original: "falqant"</note>, "the elite," and *colcothar* <note>original: "falqantār"</note>. 

All vitriols <note>original: "al-zājāt"; sulfate minerals used for their astringent properties</note> are of a substance that excels when in liquid form. *Chalkitis* and *colcothar* are found in crevices; *chalkitis* grows in certain places, *melanteria* in clusters, and "the elite" in watery places where water flows. The "dear alchemy" <note>likely referring to a refined chemical process</note> found in the matter of stone-transformation is of no use in the most specific medicinal examples. As for vitriol and its likenesses, they are of many varieties. **Galen** says that *colcothar* is a type of vitriol, though he mentions *qalqadīs* <note>white vitriol</note> specifically, which is called *chalkitis* <note>original: "khaliqītis"</note> in Greek. 

Consider our statement that *colcothar* is a variety of that which surrounds the mineral in its nature. The vitriol that is named "water" is the green vitriol which **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ibn Sīnā"; the famous Persian polymath (980–1037 AD)</note> called *falfant*, known in Greek as *misy* <note>original: "misū"; yellow vitriol</note>. Most people claim that *colcothar* grows from blue vitriol, but this is a minor error, as **Berengarius** <note>original: "al-Barinjār"; possibly a reference to a medieval translator or scholar</note> said that *colcothar* is white vitriol. This man has clearly erred in this, according to the words of **Dioscorides** <note>original: "Basfūr Durūs"</note> and **Galen** regarding them. 

As for the "contained" varieties, it is clear among them that one type is the "semen-like" vitriol <note>original: "ḥamm al-manawī"</note>, called *misy* <note>original: "manstū"</note> in Greek. Likewise, the scent is not used by the commoners who worship the "pavement vitriol." How did **Ibn Juljul** <note>original: "Ibn Juljul"; an 11th-century Andalusian physician and translator</note> say that whatever resembles it is the Greek *chalkanthos*? It is noted in the margin that on the island of **Cyprus**, in the distance, there is a copper mountain called *Polia* <note>original: "Būliyā"</note> in Greek. In it is a large chamber containing "red brick water," which flows through the earth. When we dissolve the sediment, it rises to the surface due to its heat and quality. When it dries, it is formed; I saw in it three crumbled pieces and a piece of... <note>original: "ajrū man"</note>. Its flow followed a path, and its color resembled the flow, which was extremely thick and heavy. This is the red vitriol, and that which is cooled is *misy*, and above it is a third type of red vitriol. In time, if these three eat away at something, it dries and breaks apart. I noticed in thirty years of flow that if you took a piece of that vitriol, it would fill the palm.

<meta>This page continues the pharmaceutical discussion from the previous page, shifting from the medicinal properties of raisins to the various "types" of resins and plant-derived "oils." It follows the structure of classical Greek herbalism, likely drawing from Dioscorides' *De Materia Medica* (specifically the sections on *Pithyusa* or *Euphorbium*). The text categorizes substances by their humoral qualities (heat and dryness) and their specific clinical applications for skin conditions and internal ailments.</meta>

# On Mountain Oil and Resins

**Mountain Oil** <note>original: "Zayt al-Jabal," which can refer to petroleum/bitumen, but here describes a plant-derived caustic resin</note>, which is also called **Resin**, and in Persian is known as **Mifuraj**. It contains the laxative properties of the "Mountain Herb" <note>likely a species of spurge, *Euphorbia*</note>. Among the plants that are distinguished by their growth are those with leaves like the vine, with black, upright stalks and fruit resembling the flower of the **Dhalis** <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek botanical name</note>. There is also the plant called **Sarumara Costus**, which grows thick and coarse, similar to chickpeas. Its strength is transformative, having five corners <note>referring to a pentagonal stem or seed pod</note>, and its color tends toward red and black, while its interior is white. Its quality is tested by touch.

### The Sixth Type
As for **Mountain Oil**, it is hot and dry, possessing a powerful, caustic heat as if it were a burning coal when placed upon the body. We have received word that it is used to heal [the skin] and cast out "sands" <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and it wards off the ailment where the **skin rots** <note>gangrene or necrotic ulcers</note>. Along with this power, it has a laxative quality. 

<term>Pithyusa</term> <note>original: "Basfurdurus," a corruption of the Greek *Pithyusa*, a type of spurge</note>: It is acrid; whatever it encounters, it breaks down and dries out. If it is drunk with wine, or with "water of the worms" <note>possibly a decoction used for parasites</note>, or with thick cumin and violet, it acts upon the drinker. Those who take it should have their condition managed by being given **cooked fat (ghee)** to protect them from its toxic harms. 

### The Seventh Type
This type was not fully understood from **Harush** <note>possibly a reference to a source author or a specific plant name</note>; they delayed its use for the throat. As for the fear of [internal] scarring, if it is mixed with oil, it is used for the leaves and the flesh. It thins out **lice** and treats **itchiness** and **scabies** that has not yet ulcerated. It lightens the skin and expels much phlegm. When used as a compress with vinegar, it dries out [the site] and is beneficial for **feverish pain**. If applied with honey, it heals **mouth ulcers** <note>original: "al-qula'"</note> and repels the humors of **milky tumors** <note>possibly abscesses or lymphatic swellings</note>. 

The "Mifuraj" ointment is **hot and dry in the third degree** <note>In the humoral system, the 3rd degree indicates a very potent substance that causes significant changes in the body's state</note>. It is acrid; if drunk with the water of the "fox-herb," it expels phlegm and brings satiety. If it is burnt and its smoke is inhaled, or if it is crushed and applied to a spinal orifice, it calms the pain. 

<margin>This type of resin is called "The Skewer" and its use is justified.</margin> 

If mixed with other humors, it acts as a powerful opening agent, benefiting **colic** and preventing wounds from festering. If they wish to extract blood from the temples or nostrils, it is of great benefit.

### The Fifth Type
One should know that there are five varieties. One is sponge-shaped, black, and possesses a pleasant aroma. It is one of the best for **incense**. The second variety resembles the fruit of the **pine tree** in its shape, but it is sponge-like, large, contains many seeds, and is light, with a scent similar to the "sea-claw" <note>possibly a type of seashell or operculum used in incense</note>. The third variety resembles **aloeswood** <note>original: "al-'ud"</note> in its shape and color.

<column-break/>

<margin>122</margin> 

Its color is like that of the **Berber** or the **Syrian** variety; its fruit is multicolored. This type resembles light and is full of seeds. Another type resembles a tablet in its shape and has no scent; it is generally coarse and has the form of a **mushroom** <note>original: "al-futr"</note>. It is potent and found in large quantities on the island called **Merybus** <note>likely Imbros or a similar Aegean island</note> and the lands called **Warniks**. 

Because of its origin, this type is sometimes used for **sterility**. This **Fifth Type** has volume, thickness, and a burning quality, for it is sharper than all other varieties of **Mountain Oil**, to the point that it can ignite wax. 

It is used to clear **scabies**, **freckles**, **liver spots**, and the ailment where the **skin rots**. It is used on the limbs with red ochre or with the water of the **madder plant** <note>original: "al-fuwwah"</note>. There is another variety, not mentioned before, that is superior to pomegranate; it removes marks from the face and other areas, such as **smallpox scars**. It preserves the skin from dampness, dries it, and scrapes away [dead tissue] until it reaches the sores. 

### The Third Type
This is the finest of all types. Its grains are like **pepper**, though its essence is redder. It is thin in consistency and is often found near the "fox-hole." 

### The Fourth Type
Its strength is of a singular type, though it is thinner and smaller. 

<margin>This type of resin is called "The Skewer" and its use is justified.</margin> 

It is generally called **Pithyusa** <note>original: "Sufururus/Basfurdurus"</note>. The first and second types are used for what is adjacent to them. It should be known that it is also **hot**, used to cut through **milky pustules**, **rotting of the face**, **liver spots**, and **canine rabies** <note>original: "al-kalb"</note>.

It also treats **leprosy**, **scabies in dogs**, and tumors that appear on the face. It draws blood to the area.

<margin>Its color is like some materials... smallpox, the thin neck, kidney pain, and flaccidity.</margin> 

It is used for **smallpox**, **wasting of the neck**, **kidney pain**, **flaccid flesh**, **back pain**, and pain in the posterior. It is found in wine and used in cooking. 

As for the remaining two [types], they are preserved in a vessel and may be used for other things; they dissolve and cleanse. Sometimes they dissolve [pain in] the **teeth** and help **wormwood** <note>original: "al-shih"</note> grow if mixed with salt. If they wish to extract small [stones], they pour it into the urethra. It is prepared by boiling, then covering it, and taking it out when needed. Its preparation is similar to what I mentioned regarding the oil of **lavender** <note>original: "al-khuza'i"</note>.

# On the Properties of Agaric, Ginger, and Mineral Stones

**Agaric** <term>al-ghariqun</term> <note>A wood-rotting fungus, likely *Laricifomes officinalis*, highly prized in antiquity as a purgative</note> is included in his pharmacopeia; it is of the second degree of "ferruginous" <note>dry/metallic</note> qualities and is found in locations within the lands of the Arabs. It is called *Harkud* in their dialect. Its sources are bitter, and the waters indicate many things about it, such as its use in "openers" <note>aperitifs or medicines that open blockages</note> in some of the drinks they consume in various regions, and in cooking. 

**Ginger** <term>al-zanjabil</term> consists of small roots like the roots of the *al-funun al-wafa* <note>meaning unclear, likely a local plant name</note> except that they are more solid. Its taste is similar to the taste of pepper and it is very fragrant. We should choose those that are not bland at all. Some people claim it is another type of *baqqah* <note>possibly referring to a specific gnat or a resinous residue</note> and place it in vessels to be transported even to lands where the water suitable for eating is scarce. 

He concluded his speech on its types; among those who claimed there is a lighter version, it is the one whose whiteness is greenish. The philosophers and the masters of plant knowledge brought it from the lands of India. Its births <note>varieties</note> vary, but the highest is the "deep" kind, which is powerful and the most pungent. Its seeds increase the heat just as **Black Pepper** and **Long Pepper** <note>original: "dar filfil"</note> do. It should be noted that it is powerful in its thinning <note>diluting</note> properties, but we introduce it into our medicines gradually. It is not correct to substitute it with the oil of *al-surayj* <note>lamp oil</note> because of its coldness, nor with **Verdigris** <term>al-zanjar</term> <note>Copper acetate, used topically for wounds</note>. Burnt verdigris corrodes and spreads quickly because of the "muscular moisture" it contains and its increased rapid erosion. 

Often, for the sake of pure decoration and ornamentation, these things are mentioned together because they act through sharp heat and moisture. Verdigris and Long Pepper, when soaked in bread-water, are lighter than the pleasure of the sharp heat from burnt pepper, yet stronger. Just as fire, when fueled by dry coals, ignites and spreads in the place, it cauterizes the load with a sharp heat without blood, which gives it a special power in cleaning a wound and makes its duration last longer. The sharp heat without bloodiness, which is inherited from muscular moisture, is like a wound that we want to heal from the inside. Therefore, there is room for every one of the body's wounds to be treated by its specific dye <note>medicinal application</note>. Thus, when you want the whole science to be saturated with its dye, you should present it firmly, at the moment the blood's heat is nullified in its nourishment to the site. If it decorates a limb or parts of a limb, it should be kept away from its opposite. I mean that one should also use a substance that calms the heat so that if its heat follows, it does not cause great pain, especially if the suffering is from the "silent pepper" <note>possibly a less pungent variety</note>.

### Ginger

**Ginger** <note>original: "Zanjabīl"</note> is of two types: natural and manufactured. The natural type is called in Greek ***miseron*** <note>original: "misrūn"</note>, which is bitter to the taste. The manufactured type is called in Greek ***qasīnā madārī*** <note>original: "qasīnā madārī", possibly a corruption of a term for cinnamon or a specific bark</note>. They are prepared from wild varieties and the humidity of the thickets <unclear>by aging and caution</unclear>. It is purified and its container is tightly sealed so that moisture does not ruin it entirely and waste its wisdom. From the bitterness of the *bahim* <note>possibly a livestock reference or a specific plant part</note>, it is left for a day and a night and does not change. In its fifth essence, what was claimed of old is moistened: it and the substance cut from a single plant in their treatment. Among them are the ten secrets: either ginger or the trials that are treated for days from a hidden exit of time, which is called *Arbakhor* <note>possibly a seasonal name or a specific preparation period</note>. It becomes a dark color; if the leaf flies with it, it becomes a very rough white color and is cast into the fire. There is no other known way to work it other than the material of the "ox's eye" <note>original: "bājanīyah al-thawr", likely the herb Anthemis or a similar botanical</note> when dyed. If it is hastened into food, it emits a scent like that of almonds, blended but not woody. The moist-natured ones who work with it buy its varieties due to its fine quality, called in Greek <insert>Persina</insert>. Because of this, they cannot stick to it from the moment they smell its scent, and it has the form of the *sannūr* <note>possibly a cat-like shape or a specific botanical vessel</note> and the image by which they know it. As for the *sanbarī* variety, it comes from the lands called *Liwi* <note>possibly Libya or a specific region</note>; it is valued for its action despite its scarcity and resistance to cultivation. Therefore, those who need it to be ignited did not lack the fulfillment of their needs from it.

...ascending like sulfur, and its speed in the fire is known to be of the ninth degree in strength.

### The Power of Ginger

It has a sharp power that also stimulates moisture, acts as a laxative for the head, and has a purging power like that of frogs <note>historical reference to "frog-power" often meant a specific cooling or drawing effect</note>. It is prepared for use in eye medicines because its strength is safer than that of the "frogs" <note>likely a specific medicinal compound named after the animal</note> in terms of benefit. For this reason, in the case of "fire-flesh" and cold, it stops bleeding and enters the mouth, and is effective against the burns of fire. It most benefits the "wings" <note>likely the pterygium or a growth in the eye</note> because of its dye; it is hot and dry at the end of the third degree. Others have said it is in the second degree in benefiting abscesses and the erosion of flesh in ulcers. It prevents tooth decay, dissolves bad breath from the mouth, treats chronic inflammations and putrid ulcers, and is used as a food additive over any ulcer that shows signs of decay.

### Zahrun

He said regarding the medicine called in Greek ***aelios*** <note>original: "a'liyūs," possibly referring to a sun-associated herb or Helios</note>: it is recognized by its coldness. It is also said of this type that it is "the second in coldness" from the flow of the seeds. From the Great [Books], that which is in Greek corresponds to ***al-zādiyah*** <note>possibly a reference to 'stadeia' or a measurement</note>, meaning the small sheep. *Natāris* in Greek is ***al-hamaj*** <note>small gnats/flies, perhaps a reference to the appearance of the seeds</note>. Its value is for its tree in the land of *Anthari*, which is ***al-ghurayfiyyah***. Its plant is prominent in the lands of the *Aqdām* mountains, known as ***al-darī'ah al-maghuwiyyah***. Often, it is not of the aforementioned quality; most of its growth is toward the valley. Similarly, the Ginger that is also beneficial for pregnancy is in *Masfur* <note>possibly a location</note> and its light is dim. Whatever body part has lost its scent, it is used as a construction like an ointment. It is placed upon the leaves of the *Safi'* and the *Bayan* which is called ***malūmī***. It is a source and a center, and I say of its comfort in medicines: the part of it used is weak in its color, tending toward white, and of a fine scent mixed with the dye of the laurel scent. It benefits greatly when the body or putrid areas are being "eaten." If the parts are gathered with water, it benefits those overwhelmed by a disease occurring in the muscles and their extremities. Along with breathing and the planted healing from above, and from those that are renewed or retained. Horsemen may take it from the black variety to reach a gathering of two <unclear>rähir</unclear>. What is secret in the face is surprising; if this whiteness is cleared, it agrees with it. It is beneficial for pains in the side if the liver is very swollen. Its leaf is as if it were cold; if it is pulled on a day of harm, it treats sharp, fresh inflammation. From the images of water that occur, the pouring is at its beginning, and the swelling subsides at the time of death. It also benefits as an electuary <term>la'ūq: a lickable medicinal paste</term> of almonds and nuts.

Description of the preparation of **Wool Fat**, which is called in Greek **Oesypus** <note>original: "uysīfus," the fatty substance from sheep's wool, known today as lanolin</note>. It is that which is extracted from sheep's wool before it is washed.

Wool fat is frothed and stirred with a whisk repeatedly until its foam is gathered. Then, seawater is poured over its washings. As for its scum and foam, all of it is kept refined and set aside. Stir it after pouring the water that was in it into that bitter water, and extract it from it. When the bitterness is known, pour another water over it. Repeat this many times until it is purified and becomes white. 

When its odor is removed, it becomes like a stored treasure. Let the water be hot. One must dip a piece of linen cloth to take the wool and wash it, doing so many times. Extract it and set it aside. Boil the water in a vessel, then let it cool in a night-vessel. What comes out of the oil/fat should be washed in water as we mentioned, then gathered and placed in a ceramic vessel into which hot water has been poured. Cover it with a tight ceramic lid and place it in the sun until mid-morning. It remains in the sun from one day to the next until it is purified. The best is the old variety, provided it does not smell of *Asfazyun* <note>a foul or specific chemical odor</note>. If it is old, an empty scent <note>possibly meaning neutral or light</note> wafts from it.

Its paste is also mentioned for the bite of the *Hanakah* <note>a type of lizard or small snake</note>. 

In the **Fifth [Book]**, which we have expanded upon, it is given and "the two chickens" <note>possibly a metaphor or specific medical tool/dose</note> eat it. It is recommended for the hungry person suffering from fever, in doses ranging from one <term>dirham</term> to forty <note>this likely refers to a total batch weight or a very diluted preparation</note>. **Abarsiya** is a substance that settles on the stalk <note>original: "al-azm," literally "the bone," but in botanical contexts often refers to the woody stalk or stem</note>. Sugar differs according to its consistency. Some of it is "Farukni" sugar <note>likely "Pharaonic" or a specific regional trade name</note>, which is white, light, and has less energy for the person. If it is the "Saffu" variety of Farukni sugar, it is softer and longer-lasting. **Ushar-sugar** is the softest.

<margin>For the ear and gums</margin>
# Recipe for Silt Ointment: 
Take choice pieces of pure **myrrh gum**, completely peeled of its bark and processed until it becomes like **fat**. It is described as an agent that regenerates flesh and is highly effective. It is beneficial for corrosive ailments of the <gloss>ear and gums</gloss>. It provides support and nourishment to parts of the body that have lost their vitality. In winter, it is very effective when used roasted or grilled; its pain-relieving qualities are well-regarded, though some aspects were not fully grasped by **Dioscorides** <note>original: "Basfurid," a common scribal corruption of Dioscorides</note>. Some say it is more effective than <term>Crocus</term><note>Saffron</note>, and its essence is powerful. Its flower is red and firm. It can be prepared with "Rainwater" <note>original: "Ma' al-Runku," likely a corruption of "Rainwater" or a specific distilled water</note> to enhance its potency. It may also be beneficial for growths in the nose <note>original: "minfar," likely referring to polyps</note> that sprout like leeks. Some people who planted it in the summer mistook it for small **colocynth** <note>a bitter desert fruit used as a purgative</note>, while others named it the "Mustard Tree." It grows as a small, rounded shrub.

<margin>From the measured water</margin>
Its essence is delicate, and its temperament is similar to that of **pomegranate blossom** <note>original: "julnar"</note>. If burned, its smoke is beneficial for those in the presence of the sick. Its consistency is like fat, possessing a contracting <note>astringent</note> quality that dries the saliva. It is used for ailments of the **stomach** and its surrounding area. If taken with warm water, it is more effective than a decoction of cumin. When it reaches the stomach, it acts as a bitter cleanser. Those who consume it find it beneficial, though some say it should be mixed with something else to temper its strength.

<margin>To dissolve scabs, sharpen the vision, and infuse for mouth ulcers</margin>
Its heat, as **Dioscorides** mentions, is of the second degree. It is difficult to consume on its own, so it is often shaped into pieces the size of half a **mustard seed**. It is one of the "five medicines." Some consider its highest purpose to be treating the delicate parts of the body. It removes <term>ophthalmia</term><note>eye inflammation</note> when taken with food, though it should not be applied directly to the noble skin of the eye as it causes stinging and throbbing. If a life-giving portion of it is cooked and used, it treats chronic <term>jaundice</term><note>yellowing of the skin/eyes</note> effectively. Regarding the signs of its preparation: crush it well, add **seed oil**, and it will improve the state of wounds, encouraging the growth of healthy flesh.

<margin>Clear</margin>
<margin>For chapped lips and the rest of the bowels</margin>
The most excellent kind is used to improve the eyesight and the complexion. It removes the harm caused by redness and aids the "cooling" of the body. It is followed by treatments for the **liver**, which it helps by expelling blood-like waste. It is suitable for the <term>diaphragm</term><note>original: "dhabiyya," likely the transverse muscle separating the chest from the abdomen</note>. **Galen** said regarding the liver that it acts like "karfus" <note>celery</note> or the "serpent's plant" in extracting harmful substances and relieving pain.

<margin>For sores of the temple</margin>
According to **Dioscorides**, in the second degree, if eaten, it stops the traces of illness. For the ears, it is the primary remedy for pains in the front of the head and the mouth. It is also used for **toothache**; this is extracted by boiling it in water and using the "iron-water" <note>water in which hot iron was quenched</note>. Specifically, the **Silt** ointment is disliked by some for the gums or the palate, but when mixed with olive oil, it is applied with a swab to alleviate heat and the pain of fever. If you test it, you will find it drives away "the snakes of the land" <note>metaphor for sharp, crawling pains</note> and heals the wounded.

<margin>For hearing sounds and the benefit of ear-drops</margin>
If cooked with its weight in grease and used as a rinse, it benefits tooth and gum pain and relieves tremors. If drunk with a decoction of water at the weight of one **dirham**, it assists in cases of severe <term>dropsy</term><note>edema/swelling</note> and is a boon for the ears.

<margin>Mashq (Red Ocher)</margin>
<margin>Egg white with gum</margin>

It is said that for those who suffer from **alopecia** <note>original: "al-tha'lab," literally "the fox," referring to patchy hair loss</note>, its benefit is found in applying a portion of it. # Pine Seeds <note>original: "Hub al-Sanawbar"</note>

Pine seeds are hot and dry in the second degree <note>in medieval medicine, drugs were classified into four degrees of intensity</note>. They produce a thick, viscous humor, which can be corrected by drinking a syrup made of roots. One variety of "Sinab" <note>a pungent, mustard-like condiment</note> is also hot and dry; it aids natural heat and dries out excessive moisture. It has a brittle quality and its type is easily recognized. It strengthens the inner heart. If mixed with "Prophetic medicines," it is disliked by some, as they believe it should be used to correct the individual’s specific constitution. The most common dosage when taken alone is between one to three dirhams daily, and when cooked, the weight should be between four to seven dirhams. When its aromatics are boiled and brought close, it gently expels phlegm. It is beneficial for pains in the back and the hips.

# Spikenard <note>original: "Sunbul," referring to Nardostachys jatamansi</note>

Spikenard is of three types: Indian Spikenard (called "Sunbul al-Tayyib" or Fragrant Nard), Horned Spikenard (which is Meccan Nard), and Stick Nard. Some varieties are hybrid, some are wild, and some are "fiery." One type grows in the mountains of Syria <note>original: "al-Sur"</note>, while another is called Indian because it is found there. In the lands of the Romans <note>the Byzantine Empire</note>, there is a variety called "Hona" and another called "Malam of the East." The best quality is that which is light in weight but large in volume, of a reddish-blonde color leaning towards a very light shade, with a scent reminiscent of thyme. 
A small amount of Spikenard restores eyesight and adds weight to the body if drunk with a pungent wine. As for what is called "Stick Nard," it is also known as "Cassa Tolefis" <note>likely a corruption of a Greek botanical name</note>. Its roots are found in the "Ashim" waters of the mountains of Rajan—the mountain called "Abs." The variety that grows in the "Irq" <note>lowlands or riverbeds</note> is a strong variety. The plant is smooth and straight, mostly consisting of the spike. These spikes emerge from a single root. It is often wound together for its fragrance. Some grow inside the mountain and emerge from the hills; these have the strongest scent in the fibers of the spike, smelling somewhat like a francolin <note>a type of bird, perhaps referring to a musky scent</note>. It is useful for everything we have described in the history of the Ghor region. There are also small pieces called "Seder roots" that grow on trees. As for the variety often confused with Spikenard, it is used to keep away the cold as a dye, but it may have a covering with a scent like anise. This type should be rejected. When placed near fire, it has a bitter taste, but not excessively so.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Nabataean Sciatica seed; combining the two is excellent</margin>

As for the variety found in the expected lands, the best of it is powerful for digestion, so much so that some place it under the soles of the feet. It is often used for clothing as a preservative. One must take precautions with it; wearing the fabric [treated with] its water is a powerful defense.

# The Noble Seed <note>original: "Hub al-Nabil," likely referring to Laurel or a similar prestigious berry</note>

This is the "Nabil." It was mentioned in the "Coolness [of the Eye]" as being the size of a corn kernel. This variety grows round <margin>the lion</margin> like celery, which resembles corn in the "War of Pain," God willing.

# Celery Seed <note>original: "Hub al-Karafs"</note>

A vineyard-like seed, pungent like Mahlab. It is easy to mix and is common in the Arab lands. It is a remedy for pain, God willing, and its strength is similar to a kernel of corn.

# Garden Cress Seed <note>original: "Hub al-Rashad"</note>

A white, hot seed, round in shape, and its strength is beneficial.

# Mahlab Seed <note>original: "Hub al-Mahlab," St. Lucie Cherry</note>

Also called "Akar," used for eggplant-related ailments <note>possibly referring to skin conditions</note>, eye diseases, and kidney diseases. It prevents chest pain and is beneficial. It is used for eye treatments, God willing, and helps induce perspiration during fevers.

# Laurel Seed <note>original: "Hub al-Ghar"</note>

As strong as a falcon. It is pungent, God willing. A dose the size of a "Katmiel" grain in tablet-water is hot and dry. It is very beneficial for intestinal ulcers. Its fuzz alone, [mixed with] animal water, is hotter than that of all difficult animals. Its skin is useful for gout and joints. Like other treatments, its medicine is known by its color and what lies beneath it. In general, it is used for variety of joint pains and gout.

# Eggplant Seed <note>original: "Hub al-Badhinjan"</note>

The reliable scholar Abu Hanifa <note>Abu Hanifa al-Dinawari, a famous 9th-century botanist</note> stated that it [is effective]. It is said that the "Raven's Seed" and "Marw" <note>an aromatic herb, likely Marjoram</note> strengthen the remedies for Sciatica. The Meccan variety is different in its substance; when "Marw" is mixed with it and left overnight, it becomes excellent. It is said that in science, it is a remedy for joint ailments, especially in the bones. When its leaves are scattered on the mountain, it produces seventy-seven seeds.

# Sciatica Seed <note>original: "Hub al-Nisa," likely Hermodactyl or Suranjan</note>

And Cress is also beneficial and a diuretic. Regarding this type, I did not want to add anything until the vessels contain them. Its leaf is mixed with enemas to increase its benefit. # On the Properties of Celery and Grains

<margin>Celery is among the benefits for roasted meat</margin>

**Al-Razi** <note>original: "al-Razi"; referring to Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865–925 CE), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential figures in the history of medicine</note> stated in his book *On Warding Off the Harmful Effects of Foodstuffs* that celery is beneficial when eaten with roasted meat, <unclear>unlike</unclear> when it is boiled in cold water. In terms of its qualities, it penetrates [the system] and its filtered water is cooler than both [the raw and boiled forms] and produces more gas <note>original: "riyah"; literally "winds," referring to flatulence or gastric vapors in the humoral system</note>. 

Regarding the use of pomegranate water <note>original: "ma' al-za'"; likely referring to sour pomegranate or a similar acidic liquid</note> for weakness: one should take parched wheat flour <note>original: "sawiq al-hinta"; a traditional staple made by parching grain then grinding it</note>, though parched barley flour is especially good and penetrates well. By repeatedly passing through the stomach, its benefit to the stomach is enhanced if it is boiled thoroughly in water. It should then be gathered in a thin cloth so the water may drain, and then squeezed until the residue is clear. In this state of transformation and in "cold" conditions <note>referring to the humoral temperament</note>, it moves [the humors], excites heat, and is beneficial for cases of **scabies** <note>original: "jarab"; a term used for various itchy skin eruptions</note>. 

Its consumption should be prevented for those with excessive modesty <note>possibly a transcription error or a reference to a psychological state</note>, but in general, they mentioned its specific properties. It is not suitable for those suffering from conditions like <term>hidayya</term> <note>likely a term for a specific type of swelling or protrusion</note>, or those with kidney issues or delusions, as it may tax the limbs. As for those of a "cold" constitution, it aids their vision, joint pains, chronic aches, and <term>mashaj</term> <note>likely referring to griping or intestinal cramps</note>. Most cold temperaments are not harmed by it; rather, it benefits them. 

The green variety is particularly effective; they should cleanse themselves with it after chewing it, or use it as a liniment for the raw flesh. After a third [of the treatment], they should apply it with parched barley flour. Although barley flour is colder than wheat flour, wheat flour is used more due to how it moves through the passages.

<margin>Slow to digest and causes bloating</margin>

Since it is slow to digest and causes bloating, a lighter preparation is more effective for aches and pains. These current treatments in the "House of the Great Family" are intended for... <note>the text here seems to refer to a specific hospital or noble household pharmacy</note>. The first requirement is that the receptive nature of the patient be considered. It is easier to describe it as a path; it is not a superior cooling food in the way that barley flour is. 

In the "Fifth Age" <note>likely a reference to a stage of life or a specific medical timeframe</note>, the nature of the body should be balanced with heat. Wheat flour is better for the nature of the sea [climates]. As for parched barley flour, when pomegranate water is unavailable, it treats dryness and dampness of the stomach, and types of **yellow bile** <note>one of the four humors, associated with heat and dryness</note> arising from burning sensations. It helps the "tablets" <note>medicinal lozenges</note> pass through the sharpest [passages], and benefits the mouth of the stomach. 

Barley flour is a food except when used as a medicine, in which case it is cooked into a broth and washed with sweet substances—the best and most specific of which is honey. This stops that which causes the "shaking" of the limbs. When its appearance is clarified and it is well-known, it benefits against stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>... 

Regarding the seeds of **Cumin** and **Sesely** <note>original: "Sisamaliyun"; likely *Seseli*, a genus of herbaceous plants used medicinally</note>: **Dioscorides** <note>the 1st-century Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> says in his third book that it is similar in meaning to <unclear>bitter</unclear> and its command is... it grows in cultivated land and resembles the <unclear>Faniyan</unclear>.

<column-break/>

...one of its seeds, which prevents [certain] ailments. **Galen** <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician</note> says in his third book of *On Simple Medicines* that this drug has a subtle, dissolving power; it heats and dries in the **third degree**. It is also considered a subtle heating agent. 

Regarding **Sisymbrion** <note>original: "Sismaron"; likely referring to *Sisymbrium*, a genus including water-parsnip or wild mints</note>: indeed, people are healed by its mixture or by its individual color. This is from **Dioscorides**, who states it has a heating and supplying power when mixed with drinks. It is used specifically for recurring fevers, being a sugar for the dusty and [those with] fevers. Its leaves are applied as a poultice on hot, benign tumors of the temple, and it is used for the stings of wasps and <unclear>insects</unclear>. 

Dioscorides says in his second book that its root, when it yields milk, is good for the stomach and stimulates the appetite for food. It also acts as a diuretic. Galen says in his eighth book that its root is even more beneficial for the stomach and for inducing urination. It is "warm" in the third degree, and contains a substance that cleanses the gallbladder. 

In some translations of **Sisymbrion**, it is called "pepper," and it was said to be like a bitter <term>kafaj</term> <note>a type of condiment or preserved relish</note> because it has no leaves. However, both Dioscorides and Galen state that *Sisymbrion* is "pepper," so consider this carefully. **Al-Razi** says in *The Comprehensive Book* <note>original: "al-Hawi"; Rhazes' massive medical encyclopedia</note> that some say *Sismaron* is the water of the wood of Cyperus, but this is far from the truth because *Sismaron* is [actually] the <unclear>qatil</unclear>. 

The **Black Seed** <note>original: "al-Shuniz"; Nigella sativa</note> does not have a "cold" description. The part used is its seed. What is used from the *Sismaron* is its root, and there is a difference in degree between them. It is best to say that *Sismaron* is the root... search until it is verified, God Willing.

There is a garden variety and it often grows in the middle of... it is beneficial for the stomach and has a scent.

It is called **Sea Tongue** <term>Lisan al-Bahr <gloss>literally "Tongue of the Sea"; the internal shell of the cuttlefish</gloss></term>. On some coasts of the Maghreb <note>North Africa</note>, it is known as *al-Fellaha*, or by names containing the letters Qaf and Nun. The common people call it *Qad* or *Yusr*. It is used for scrubbing, in the style of the people of Jerusalem. Its internal sac is shaped like a bony rod; it acts as a **laxative** for the stomach. If the stone-like substance from its interior is crushed, it serves as a liniment for **roughness of the eyelids**, tumors, and **scabies**. It is also used for sores of the mouth.

If the cover is removed from it, we use it to treat **freckles** and pustules; if it is sprinkled or rubbed, it benefits the eyes. If it is <unclear>crushed</unclear> and placed in the eyes of livestock, it heals them. If they eat much of this salted fish, it cures the **shivers** <note>original: "al-quffa"; a feverish chill</note>. **Galen** <note>original: "Jalianos"; the 2nd-century Greek physician</note> stated in the eighth book of *Simple Medicines* that those who use the sea water [from it] rub it on for severe flaccidness. Unlike others, the **snail** <note>original: "al-halazun"</note> has a specific character... and the <unclear>grain/yield</unclear> is common in the river for the *Lamia* <note>a type of shark or mythical sea creature</note> and others, according to the refinement and repetition of the physician.

As for the aerial matter, it is found in the Maghreb during the summer. Therefore, it is used as an extract to treat **pimples**, **freckles**, lethargy, and scabies. It is also combined with vinegar and strong salt to heal the **pterygium** <note>original: "al-zafara"; a fleshy growth on the white of the eye</note> before it spreads. Furthermore, when sprinkled or rubbed on moist sores of the groin or the <unclear>scrotum</unclear>, it is very effective. The medicinal water is also used for moderate roughness; it is used for scrubbing when there is severe roughness, applied with a dressing. One may rub the inside of the eyelid until it bleeds slightly, for experience shows that this action is among the best **eye-pellets** <term>Shiyafat <gloss>medicated pastes or suppositories shaped like seeds, used for eye treatments</gloss></term> for the eye. In the sea-foam, there are many uses: it is taken from the sea water and mixed with salt for **alopecia** <note>original: "da' al-tha'lab"; literally "fox disease"</note> and <unclear>skin peeling</unclear>, as it has a cleansing power...

## Al-Ghawab
A type of offering called *Kanimir*—
It is the *Dalyutio*, mentioned once under the letter *Dal*. The **Salamander** <note>original: "Samandar"</note> is under the letter *Seen*. I have already mentioned it under the letter *Kha*. *Sikar* or the "Nubian" in Arabic; I mentioned it under the letter *Ya*. This medicine is named so because it is used to treat... it is sprinkled on a stone and mixed with its water until it is blended, then used for the pain of... <unclear>the water</unclear>.

<margin>
A fish in the salt sea <unclear>cannot be found</unclear>
A fish
For him every week
